He said: *al-ṣarf* (declension with tanwin) is more beloved to me, since I have not found a parallel to this altered form.

It was also said that *Ṭuwā* means "O man" in Hebrew, so it is as if it were said: "O man, go!" It was also said that the meaning is: the sacred valley was blessed twice, and the first meaning is preferable.

The detailed discussion of this has already passed.

﴿اذْهَبْ إلى فِرْعَوْنَ إنَّهُ طَغى﴾ ("Go to Pharaoh; indeed he has transgressed") — it was said this is under an implied *qawl* (saying), and it was said it is an explanation of the calling: that is, He called him with a call which is His saying "Go." It was also said it is under the omission of the explanatory *an* (أنْ), and this is supported by Ibn Mas'ud's reading ﴿أنِ اذْهَبْ﴾, because a call carries the meaning of saying. The clause ﴿إنَّهُ طَغى﴾ ("indeed he has transgressed") is a justification for the command, or for the obligation of obedience: that is, he exceeded the limit in disobedience, arrogance and disbelief in Allah.

Then say to him ﴿هَلْ لَكَ إلى أنْ تَزَكّى﴾ ("Would you like to purify yourself?"), that is, His saying, after your arrival to him: is there in you a desire for purification (tazakkī), which is cleansing oneself from polytheism. Its original form is *tatazakkā*, and one of the two *tā'* was deleted.

The majority read *tazakkā* with a light (takhfif) pronunciation. Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read it with the *zāy* doubled, through assimilating the *tā'* into the *zāy*.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: the meaning of the light reading is "that you become pure and believing," and the meaning of the doubled reading is "giving charity (ṣadaqah)." In the sentence there is an implied subject (mubtada' muqaddar) to which *ilā* is attached, and the estimate is: "Is there in you a desire, or is there in you an inclination, or is there in you a path to purification?" Similar to this is the saying of people: *hal laka fi al-khayr?* ("Is there for you in goodness?") meaning: "Is there for you a desire for goodness?" From this is the saying of the poet:

؎ فَهَلْ لَكَمَ فِيها إلَيَّ فَإنَّنِي ∗∗∗ بَصِيرٌ بِما أعْيا النِّطاسِيَّ جَذِيمًا

"Then is there for you (to come) to me in this matter? Indeed I am skilled in what baffled the physician Jadhīm."

﴿وأهْدِيَكَ إلى رَبِّكَ فَتَخْشى﴾ ("and I would guide you to your Lord, so you would fear Him") — that is, I would guide you to His worship and His unity, so that you would fear His punishment. The *fā'* (so) indicates the sequence of fear upon guidance, because fear cannot be except from one who is guided and rightly guided.

﴿فَأراهُ الآيَةَ الكُبْرى﴾ ("Then he showed him the greatest sign") — this *fā'* is the *fā' faṣīḥah* (the eloquent *fā'*), because it reveals an omitted speech. The meaning is: so he went and said to him what he said, as Allah related in more than one place, and he (Pharaoh) answered him with what he answered, until he said ﴿إنْ كُنْتَ جِئْتَ بِآيَةٍ فَأْتِ بِها﴾ ("If you have come with a sign, then produce it") [al-A'raf: 106]. At that point he showed him the greatest sign.

They differed regarding what the greatest sign was. It was said: the staff; it was said: his hand; it was said: the splitting of the sea; and it was said: it is all of the nine signs he brought.

﴿فَكَذَّبَ وعَصى﴾ ("But he denied and disobeyed") — that is, when he showed him the greatest sign, he denied Moses and what he brought and disobeyed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so he did not obey Him.

﴿ثُمَّ أدْبَرَ﴾ ("Then he turned his back") — that is, he turned away and withdrew from faith. ﴿يَسْعى﴾ ("striving") — that is, he worked at corruption upon the earth and strove to oppose what Moses brought. It was also said: *adbara* means he fled from the serpent, hastening out of fear of it.

Al-Razi said: the meaning of ﴿أدْبَرَ يَسْعى﴾ is "he came forward, hastening," just as one says *aqbala yaf'alu kadhā*, meaning "he began to do such-and-such." So *adbara* was put in the place of *aqbala* so that he would not be described as advancing.

﴿فَحَشَرَ﴾ ("Then he gathered") — that is, he gathered his troops for fighting and warfare, or gathered the magicians for opposition, or gathered the people to be present to witness what would happen, or gathered them so that they might protect him from the serpent.

﴿فَنادى فَقالَ أنا رَبُّكُمُ الأعْلى﴾ ("And he proclaimed, saying, 'I am your most exalted lord'") — that is, he said to them with a loud voice, or he ordered someone to proclaim this statement.

The meaning of ﴿أنا رَبُّكُمُ الأعْلى﴾ is that there is no lord above me.

ʻAṭāʼ said: he had made for them small idols and ordered them to worship them, and said: "I am the lord of your idols." It was also said that by his being their lord he meant that he was their leader and their master.

The first is preferable, because of His saying in another verse: ﴿ما عَلِمْتُ لَكم مِن إلَهٍ غَيْرِي﴾ ("I know of no god for you other than me") [al-Qasas: 38].

﴿فَأخَذَهُ اللَّهُ نَكالَ الآخِرَةِ والأُولى﴾ ("So Allah seized him, the punishment of the Hereafter and of this world") — *nakāl* is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun: that is, He seized him with a seizing of punishment; or it is a verbal noun of an omitted verb: that is, Allah seized him and made an example of him, the punishment of the Hereafter and the first; or it is an emphatic verbal noun for the content of the sentence. By "the punishment of the Hereafter" is meant the torment of the Fire, and "the punishment of the first" is the torment of this world by drowning.

Mujahid said: the torment of the beginning of his life and its end.

Qatadah said: the "Hereafter" is His saying ﴿أنا رَبُّكُمُ الأعْلى﴾, and the "first" is his denial of Moses.

It was also said: the "Hereafter" is His saying ﴿أنا رَبُّكُمُ الأعْلى﴾, and the first is His saying ﴿ما عَلِمْتُ لَكم مِن إلَهٍ غَيْرِي﴾. Between the two statements there were forty years.

It is permissible for *nakāla* to be in the accusative as an object of purpose (mafʻūl lahu): that is, Allah seized him for the sake of an example. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative by removing the preposition: that is, "with a punishment."

Al-Zajjaj preferred that it is an emphatic verbal noun, saying: because the meaning of "Allah seized him" is "Allah made an example of him with him," so it is derived from its meaning and not from its wording.

Al-Farra' said: that is, Allah seized him with a seizing of *nakāl*, i.e., for the sake of punishment. *Al-nakāl* is the name of what is made a punishment for others, i.e., a penalty for him. It is said *nakkala fulān bi-fulān* when he punished him.

The origin of the word is from restraint, and from it comes *al-nukūl ʻan al-yamīn* (refusing to take an oath), and *al-nakl* is a fetter.

﴿إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَعِبْرَةً لِمَن يَخْشى﴾ ("Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears") — that is, in what has been mentioned of the story of Pharaoh and what was done to him is a great lesson for one whose nature is to fear Allah and be mindful of Him, to fear His punishment and to beware of His anger.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʻAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib regarding His saying ﴿والنّازِعاتِ غَرْقًا﴾ ("By those who drag out with violence"): he said: they are the angels who draw out the souls of the disbelievers. ﴿والنّاشِطاتِ نَشْطًا﴾ ("and those who draw out gently"): he said: they are the angels who draw out the souls of the disbelievers from between the nails and the skin until they bring them out. ﴿والسّابِحاتِ سَبْحًا﴾ ("and those who glide swiftly"): they are the angels who glide with the souls of the believers between heaven and earth. ﴿فالسّابِقاتِ سَبْقًا﴾ ("then those who race forward"): they are the angels, some of whom outrace others with the souls of the believers to Allah. ﴿فالمُدَبِّراتِ أمْرًا﴾ ("then those who arrange affairs"): they are the angels who arrange the affairs of the servants from year to year.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʻAbbas regarding ﴿والنّازِعاتِ غَرْقًا﴾: he said: they are the souls of the disbelievers, which are drawn out, then drawn gently, then drowned in the Fire.

al-Hakim narrated and authenticated from him regarding ﴿والنّازِعاتِ غَرْقًا﴾ and ﴿والنّاشِطاتِ نَشْطًا﴾: he said: it is death.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿والنّازِعاتِ غَرْقًا﴾: he said: the angels who attend to the souls of the disbelievers. Up to His saying ﴿والسّابِحاتِ سَبْحًا﴾: he said: the angels.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Do not tear people apart, lest the dogs of the Fire tear you apart. Allah said: ﴿والناشِطاتِ نَشْطًا﴾. Do you know what it is?" I said: "O Prophet of Allah, what is it?" He said: "Dogs in the Fire that draw out flesh and bone."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʻAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib that Ibn al-Kawwa' asked him about ﴿فالمُدَبِّراتِ أمْرًا﴾, and he said: they are the angels who arrange the remembrance and command of the Most Merciful.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Dhikr al-Mawt* narrated from Ibn ʻAbbas, who said: ﴿فالمُدَبِّراتِ أمْرًا﴾: they are angels who are with the Angel of Death, attending the dead at the taking of their souls. Among them are those who raise up the soul, among them are those who say "Amen" to the supplication, and among them are those who ask forgiveness for the deceased until he is prayed over and lowered into his grave.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿يَوْمَ تَرْجُفُ الرّاجِفَةُ﴾ ("On the Day the quake will convulse"): he said: it is the first blast. ﴿تَتْبَعُها الرّادِفَةُ﴾ ("followed by the second"): he said: the second blast. ﴿قُلُوبٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ واجِفَةٌ﴾ ("Hearts that Day will be pounding"): he said: fearful. ﴿أئِنّا لَمَرْدُودُونَ في الحافِرَةِ﴾ ("Shall we indeed be returned to our former state?"): he said: life.

Ahmad, ʻAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it ḥasan), Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *Shuʻab al-Iman* narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "When a quarter of the night had passed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would rise and say: 'O people, remember Allah! The quake has come, followed by the second; death has come with what it carries.'"

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The earth will quake with a great quaking, and its inhabitants will be shaken. It is the one of which Allah says: ﴿يَوْمَ تَرْجُفُ الرّاجِفَةُ تَتْبَعُها الرّادِفَةُ﴾." He said: "Like a ship on the sea that tilts with its people, like a lamp suspended by its sides."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʻAbbas regarding ﴿قُلُوبٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ واجِفَةٌ﴾: he said: frightened and agitated.

ʻAbd ibn Humayd narrated from him regarding ﴿أئِنّا لَمَرْدُودُونَ في الحافِرَةِ﴾: he said: a new creation.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 79, verse 1–26 (part 3 of 3):

Abu 'Ubayd (d. 224 AH) in his Fada'il (Virtues of the Qur'an), Ibn al-Anbari in al-Waqf wa'l-Ibtida' (Stopping and Starting), 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim all narrated from him (Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him), also, that he was asked about the words of Allah: ﴿So they will be upon the surface of the earth﴾ and he said: "al-Sahirah is the surface of the earth." In another wording he said: "The whole earth is sahirah. Do you not see the saying of the poet:
"The game of the sea and the game of the sahirah"

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat also narrated from him, regarding the words ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ that he said: "Would you like to say: There is no god but Allah?"

Ibn Jarir also narrated from him regarding ﴿So Allah seized him in the punishment of the Hereafter and the former﴾ that he said: "It refers to his saying: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾, and the former (al-ula) refers to his saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas: 38]."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr that he said: "Between his two words there were forty years."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 79, verses 1–26 (part 1 of 3):

It is Meccan, without any disagreement.

Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Nazi'at was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Allah, glorified is He, swore by these things He mentioned, which are the angels who draw out the souls of the servants from their bodies, as one who draws a bow pulls it until he reaches its full extent. Likewise, what is meant by "al-nashitat" (those who unfasten), "al-sabihat" (those who glide) and "al-sabiqat" (those who outstrip) and "al-mudabbirat" (those who arrange affairs) is the angels. The conjunction (of these descriptions) with the unity of the referent is to treat the difference in attributes as if it were a difference in essence, as in the words of the poet:

"To the stern king, and the son of the brave hero, and the lion of the battalion in the crowded press."

This is the view of the majority of the Companions (Sahabah), the Successors (Tabi'un) and those after them.

al-Suddi said: "al-Nazi'at are the souls when they sink into the chests."

Mujahid said: "They are death, drawing out the soul."

Qatadah said: "They are the stars that draw from one horizon to another, from the saying 'nazaʻa ilayhi' (he went toward it) when he departed, or from the saying 'nazaʻat bil-habl' (she pulled with the rope), meaning that they set, disappear and rise from another horizon."

Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Akhfash and Ibn Kaysan held the same view.

'Ata' and 'Ikrimah said: "al-Nazi'at are the bows which draw the arrows. The extreme drawing of the one who draws the bow is that he pulls it to its full extent until it reaches the arrowhead."

Yahya ibn Salam said: "They draw (the animals) between the pastures and make them flee." It was also said that by al-Nazi'at he meant the raiding archers.

The accusative of "gharqan" is that it is a verbal noun (masdar) with its extra letters omitted, meaning "ighraqan" (extreme). Its governing verb is what precedes it, because it corresponds to it in meaning, meaning: extremity in drawing, in that they draw them from the farthest parts of the bodies. Or it is in the accusative of state, meaning: possessing extremity. It is said "aghraqa fi al-shay'" (he went to the extreme in the matter) when one goes deep into it and reaches its utmost limit.

The meaning of "wal-nashitat" is that they unfasten the souls, meaning they bring them out of the bodies, as a tether is unfastened from the foot of a camel when it is untied. It is said "nashaṭa al-rajul al-dalw min al-bi'r" (the man drew the bucket out of the well) when he brought it out. And "al-nashat" is pulling swiftly, and from it comes "al-unshuta" (the slip-knot), the knot which is easy to undo.

Abu Zayd said: "nashatu al-habl, anshuṭuhu, nashaṭan" means I tied it, and "anshaṭtuhu" means I untied it, and "anshaṭtu al-habl" means I stretched the rope.

al-Farra' said: "ansha al-'iqal" means it untied, and "nashiṭa" means he tied the rope on his hands.

al-Asma'i said: "Bi'r anshat" is a well whose bottom is near, from which the bucket comes out with a single pull, and "bi'r nashut" is one from which the bucket does not come out until it is pulled hard many times.

Mujahid said: "It is death, which unfastens the soul of the human being."

al-Suddi said: "They are the souls when they are unfastened from the two feet."

'Ikrimah and 'Ata' said: "They are the nooses that release the arrows." Qatadah, al-Hasan and al-Akhfash said: "They are the stars that move from one horizon to another, meaning they go away."

In al-Sihah it is said: "wal-nashitat nashtan" means the stars from one constellation to another, "like the unbridled bull from one land to another," and "the worries move their owner."

Abu 'Ubaydah and Qatadah said: "They are the wild beasts when they move from one land to another."

It was also said: "al-Nashitat" refers to the souls of the believers, and "al-Nazi'at" refers to the souls of the disbelievers, because the angel draws the soul of the believer gently and draws the soul of the disbeliever violently. His saying "nashtan" is a verbal noun, and likewise "sabhan" and "sabqan."

"Al-Sabihat" are the angels who swim in the bodies to bring out the soul, as the diver swims in the sea to bring out something from it.

Mujahid and Abu Salih said: "They are the angels who descend from the sky hastening by the command of Allah, as one says of a noble horse, 'sabih,' when it hastens in its running."

Mujahid also said: "al-Sabihat: death, which swims in the souls of the children of Adam."

It was also said: "They are the horses swimming in the raid." From this is the saying of 'Antarah:

"And the horses know, when they swim (sabh) into the cisterns of death, a swim."

Qatadah and al-Hasan said: "They are the stars which swim in their orbits, as in His saying: ﴿And each in an orbit they swim﴾ [Ya-Sin: 40]." 'Ata' said: "They are the ships which swim on the water." It was also said: "They are the spirits of the believers which swim out of longing for Allah."

﴿Then those who outstrip, outstripping﴾: they are the angels according to the view of the majority, as has passed.

Masruq and Mujahid said: "The angels outstrip the devils to the prophets with the revelation."

Abu Rawq said: "They are the angels who precede the son of Adam with good and righteous deeds." Something similar was narrated from Mujahid.

Muqatil said: "They precede with the souls of the believers to Paradise."

al-Rabi' said: "They are the souls of the believers which outstrip to the angels out of longing for Allah."

Mujahid also said: "It is death, which outstrips the human being."

Qatadah, al-Hasan and Ma'mar said: "They are the stars, some of which outstrip others in their course."

'Ata' said: "They are the horses which outstrip to the jihad."

It was also said: "They are the spirits which precede the bodies to Paradise or to the Fire."

al-Jurjani said: "He connected 'al-sabiqat' with the letter fa' because they are causes of what came before them, meaning: if you said 'he stood and went' with the letter wa', the standing would not have been a cause of the going."

al-Wahidi said: "This is not consistent in His saying: ﴿Then those who arrange affairs, arranging﴾, because it is far-fetched to make the outstripping a cause of arranging."

al-Razi said: "The answer to what al-Wahidi said is that when they were commanded, they swam, then they outstripped, then they arranged what they were commanded to arrange, so these are acts that are connected to one another, like the saying: 'Zayd stood up and then went.' When they outstripped in acts of obedience and hastened to them, their trustworthiness became apparent, so the arranging was entrusted to them."

It is answered that outstripping is not a cause of arranging, just as swimming is not a cause of outstripping and standing is not a cause of going. Mere connection does not necessitate causation and being caused.

The better view is that the conjunction with fa' in "al-mudabbirat" is made to correspond to the conjunction with fa' before it, "al-sabiqat," and it does not need a special reason as the earlier one did, because a special reason is sought only for the later differing from the earlier, not for its agreement and conformity with it.

﴿Then those who arrange affairs, arranging﴾: al-Qushayri said: "They agreed that what is meant here is the angels."

al-Mawardi said: "There are two views on this: the first is that they are the angels, which is the view of the majority. The second is that they are the seven planets, reported by Khalid ibn Ma'dan from Mu'adh ibn Jabal."

Regarding their arranging the affair, there are two views: the first is that they arrange the rising and setting of the stars. The second is arranging what Allah decreed in them of states.

The meaning of the angels' arranging the affair is their descent with the lawful and the unlawful and their detailing of them. Although the true agent of arranging is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, when the angels descended with it, it was attributed to them.

It was also said that when the angels were commanded to arrange the affairs of the people of the earth concerning winds, rains and other things, they were called "mudabbirat."

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabat said: "The arranging of the affairs of this world is entrusted to four angels: Jibril, Mika'il, 'Izra'il and Israfil. As for Jibril, he is in charge of the winds and the armies. As for Mika'il, he is in charge of rain and plants. As for 'Izra'il, he is in charge of seizing the souls. As for Israfil, he descends with the command to them."

The answer to the oath by these matters, which Allah swore by, is omitted; the meaning is: "By the drawers, and likewise, and likewise, you will surely be raised."

al-Farra' said: "It is omitted because the listeners know it, and His saying indicates it: ﴿Shall we, when we are bones decayed?﴾"

It was also said that the answer to the oath is His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾, meaning: indeed in the Day of Resurrection and the mention of Musa and Fir'awn there is a lesson for whoever fears.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "This is ugly, because the speech has been lengthy between them."

It was also said that the answer to the oath is: ﴿Has there come to you the report of Musa?﴾, because the meaning is "it has come to you." This is very weak.

It was also said that the answer is: ﴿On the Day the quaking one quakes﴾, on the assumption of: "On the Day the quaking one quakes, the following one follows."

al-Sijistani said: "It is possible that this is of inversion, as if He said: 'Then they are in the awakened place, and by the drawers.'"

Ibn al-Anbari said: "This is an error, because the fa' is not used to begin speech. The first view is better."

﴿On the Day the quaking one quakes﴾: the accusative of this time expression is by the omitted answer to the oath, or by the implied verb "remember." Al-Rajifah means the one that trembles; it is said "rajafa yarjufu" when it trembles. Here it means the great cry in which there is shaking and agitation like thunder, and it is the first blast by which all creatures die. Al-Radifah is the second blast, which occurs at the resurrection, and it was called "radifah" because it follows the first blast. This is what the majority of the exegetes said.

Ibn Zayd said: "al-Rajifah is the earth, and al-Radifah is the Hour."

Mujahid said: "al-Radifah is the earthquake, and the following one is the cry." It was also said: "al-Rajifah is the trembling of the earth and al-Radifah is the earthquake." The root of "rajfah" is movement, and the meaning is not merely movement here. Rather, al-Rajifah here is derived from the saying: "rajafa al-ra'd yarjufu rajfan wa rajifan" when the sound of the thunder appears. From this came "al-arajif" (rumours), because of the agitation of voices in them and the appearance of voices in them. From this is the saying of the poet:

"With rumours, O son of baseness, you threaten me, and in rumours I thought baseness and weakness."

The position of "tatba'uha al-radifah" (the following one follows it) is accusative as a state of "al-rajifah," and the meaning: you will surely be raised on the day of the first blast, in the state that the second blast follows it.

﴿Hearts on that Day will be trembling﴾: "qulub" is the subject, "yawma'idhin" is in the accusative governed by "wajifah," and "wajifah" is an adjective of "qulub."

The sentence ﴿their eyes will be humbled﴾ is the predicate of "qulub." al-Rajifah means agitated and restless, because of what they witnessed of the horrors of the Day of Resurrection.

The majority of the exegetes said: "That is, afraid and fearful."

al-Suddi said: "Removed from their places," similar to ﴿When hearts reach the throats﴾ [Ghafir: 18]. al-Mu'arrij said: "Restless, anxious."

al-Mubarrad said: "Agitated. It is said 'wajafa al-qalb yajifu wajifan' when it pounds, as one says 'wajaba yajibu wajiban.' The 'ijaf' is swift travel, so the root of 'wajif' is agitation of the heart."

From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"Indeed the sons of Jahjaba and their people, our livers behind them tremble."

"Their eyes will be humbled": that is, the eyes of its owners, so the possessive was omitted. "Khashi'ah" means humiliated, and what is meant is that humiliation and submission appear upon them at witnessing the horrors of the Day of Resurrection, like His saying: ﴿Humbled from humiliation﴾ [al-Shura: 45].

'Ata' said: "He means the eyes of those who died without Islam, and the context indicates this, since the context concerns those who deny resurrection."

﴿They say: "Shall we indeed be returned to the former state?"﴾: this is a report of what the deniers of resurrection say when they are told that they will be raised. That is: shall we be returned to our first condition and the beginning of our affair, so that we become alive after our death? It is said "raja'a fulan fi hafiratih," meaning he returned from where he came. al-Hafirah, among the Arabs, is the name for the beginning of a thing and the start of an affair. From this is the saying: "raja'a fulan 'ala hafiratih," meaning on the road by which he came. It is also said: "They fought at the hafirah," meaning at the first meeting. The road by which one came is called "hafirah" because of its being impressed upon it by his walking on it, so it is "hafirah" in the sense of "mahfurah" (dug out). From this is the saying of the poet:

"Shall I return on a bald head and white hair? God forbid from folly and shame."

Meaning: shall I return to what I was in my youth of amorous pursuit after white hair and baldness? It was said: "al-Hafirah" is "al-'ajilah" (the present life), and the meaning is: indeed we will be returned to the world. It was said: "al-Hafirah" is the earth in which their graves are dug. From this is the saying of the poet:

"I swore I would not forget you, so know, until people are returned to the hafirah."

The meaning: indeed we will be returned in our graves alive. So said al-Khalil and al-Farra', and Mujahid said likewise.

Ibn Zayd said: "al-Hafirah is the Fire," and he took as evidence His saying: ﴿That, then, would be a losing return﴾.

al-Jumhur read ﴿fi al-hafirah﴾, and Abu Haywah read "fi al-hufrah" (in the pit).

﴿Shall we, when we are bones decayed?﴾: that is, crumbling and disintegrating. It is said "nakhira al-'azm" (the bone decayed) when it deteriorates. This is an emphasis on the denial of resurrection: that is, how can we be returned alive and raised when we are decayed bones? The governing element in "idha" is implied, indicated by "mardudun": that is, shall we, when we are decayed bones, be returned and raised, while being the thing farthest from life?

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 79, verses 1–26 (part 2 of 3):

The majority (al-Jumhur) read *nakhirah* (نَخِرَةً). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read *nakhirah* with an alif (ناخِرَةً). Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the first reading, while al-Farra', Ibn Jarir and Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi preferred the second.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: *al-nakhirah* is the bone that has not yet been hollowed out (lam tunkhar ba'd), meaning it has not yet decayed, though it will inevitably be hollowed out.

It was also said that the two forms have the same meaning. The Arabs say *nakhira al-shay'* so it is *nākhir* and *nakhir*, and *ṭami'a* so it is *ṭāmi'* and *ṭami'*, and similar forms.

Al-Akhfash said: both are dialectal variants (lughatān), and whichever you recite is good.

The poet said:

؎ يَظَلُّ بِها الشَّيْخُ الَّذِي كانَ بادِنًا ∗∗∗ يَدُبُّ عَلى عِوَجٍ لَهُ نَخِراتُ

"The old man who was once corpulent crawls upon it, on crooked limbs that are hollowed out (nakhirāt)."

He means: on crooked legs.

It was also said that *al-nākhirah* is the bone whose extremities have been eaten away while its middle remains, and *al-nakhirah* is the bone that has entirely decayed.

Mujahid said: *nakhirah* means *marfūtah* (crumbled to dust), as in His saying ﴿رُفاتًا﴾ (dust). It has also been recited as ﴿إذا كُنّا﴾ and as ﴿أئِذا كُنّا﴾, with the interrogative and without it.

Then Allah, glorified is He, related another statement of theirs, saying: ﴿They said, "That would then be a losing return."﴾ That is, a return that brings loss to those who experience it. The meaning is that they said: if we are returned after death, we will surely suffer loss through what will befall us after death from what Muhammad says.

It was also said that the meaning of *khāsirah* is *kādhibah* (false), i.e., it will not come to pass. This is what al-Hasan and others said.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: *khāsirah* means losing for the one who denies it.

Qatadah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: that is, if we are returned after death, we will surely lose through the Fire. They only said this because they had been threatened with the Fire. *Al-karrah* means the return, and its plural is *karrāt*.

His saying ﴿فَإنَّما هي زَجْرَةٌ واحِدَةٌ﴾ ("It will be but a single blast") is a justification for what precedes it, namely their disbelief in the resurrection of the decayed bones and the revival of the dead. The meaning is: do not regard that as unlikely, for it will be but a single blast, and that will be the revival and resurrection. By *zajrah* is meant the cry (al-ṣayḥah), which is the second blast by which resurrection occurs.

It was also said that the pronoun in His saying ﴿إنَّما هي﴾ refers to *al-rādifah* mentioned earlier.

﴿فَإذا هم بِالسّاهِرَةِ﴾ ("then they will be on the surface of the earth"), that is, then the creatures who had died and been buried will be alive upon the face of the earth. Al-Wahidi said: by *al-sāhirah* is meant the face of the earth and its surface, according to the consensus.

Al-Farra' said: it was called this name because on it is the sleep and wakefulness of living creatures. It was also said that it is called this because a person stays awake in its deserts out of fear of it. From this is the saying of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali:

؎ يَرُدُّونَ ساهِرَةً كَأنَّ حَمِيمَها ∗∗∗ وغَمِيمَها أسْدافُ لَيْلٍ مُظْلِمِ

"They pass through a sāhirah whose depths and whose surface are like the dark mantles of a gloomy night."

And the saying of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt:

؎ وفِيها لَحْمُ ساهِرَةٍ وبَحْرٌ ∗∗∗ وما فاهُوا بِهِ لَهُمُ مُقِيمُ

"In it is the flesh of the sāhirah and the sea, and what they utter remains with them."

He means the flesh of the living creatures of the sāhirah land.

In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* it says: *al-sāhirah* is the face of the earth, and from this is His saying ﴿فَإذا هم بِالسّاهِرَةِ﴾.

It also says: *al-sāhirah* is a white land. It was said it is a land of silver upon which Allah, glorified is He, was never disobeyed. It was also said that *al-sāhirah* is the seventh earth, which Allah, glorified is He, will bring forth, and upon it He will call the creatures to account.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: *al-sāhirah* is the land of Syria.

Qatadah said: it is Hell (jahannam). That is: then these disbelievers will be in Hell. It is called *sāhirah* because they do not sleep in it, due to the continuity of their punishment.

The sentence ﴿هَلْ أتاكَ حَدِيثُ مُوسى﴾ ("Has there reached you the story of Moses?") is a new sentence (mustaʼnafah), brought to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding the denial of his people, and that there will befall them the like of what befell those before them who were stronger than them. The meaning of *hal atāka* is: "has there come to you and reached you?" This is on the assumption that he had heard of the stories of Pharaoh and Moses that would make him know their account. On the other assumption, that this was the first revelation to him concerning them, the meaning is interrogative: "Has there come to you the story of him? I will inform you of it."

﴿إذْ ناداهُ رَبُّهُ بِالوادِي المُقَدَّسِ طُوًى﴾ ("when his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa") — the adverbial phrase is attached to *ḥadīth* (the story), not to *atāka* (has come), because their times differ. The story of Moses and Pharaoh has already passed in more than one place, where there is sufficiency. The difference among the readers regarding *Ṭuwā* has already been mentioned in Surah Ṭā-Hā.

*Al-wādī al-muqaddas* means the blessed and purified valley.

Al-Farra' said: *Ṭuwā* is a valley between Medina and Egypt. He said: it is a *maʻdūl* (a word altered from its original form) from *ṭāwin*, just as ʻUmar is altered from ʻĀmir. He said: *al-ṣarf* (declension with tanwin) is more beloved to me, since I have not found a parallel to this altered form.

It was also said that *Ṭuwā* means "O man" in Hebrew, so it is as if it were said: "O man, go!" It was also said that the meaning is: the sacred valley was blessed twice, and the first meaning is preferable.

The detailed discussion of this has already passed.

﴿اذْهَبْ إلى فِرْعَوْنَ إنَّهُ طَغى﴾ ("Go to Pharaoh; indeed he has transgressed") — it was said this is under an implied *qawl* (saying), and it was said it is an explanation of the calling: that is, He called him with a call which is His saying "Go." It was also said it is under the omission of the explanatory *an* (أنْ), and this is supported by Ibn Mas'ud's reading ﴿أنِ اذْهَبْ﴾, because a call carries the meaning of saying. The clause ﴿إنَّهُ طَغى﴾ ("indeed he has transgressed") is a justification for the command, or for the obligation of obedience: that is, he exceeded the limit in disobedience, arrogance and disbelief in Allah.

Then say to him ﴿هَلْ لَكَ إلى أنْ تَزَكّى﴾ ("Would you like to purify yourself?"), that is, His saying, after your arrival to him: is there in you a desire for purification (tazakkī), which is cleansing oneself from polytheism. Its original form is *tatazakkā*, and one of the two *tā'* was deleted.

The majority read *tazakkā* with a light (takhfif) pronunciation. Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read it with the *zāy* doubled, through assimilating the *tā'* into the *zāy*.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: the meaning of the light reading is "that you become pure and believing," and the meaning of the doubled reading is "giving charity (ṣadaqah)." In the sentence there is an implied subject (mubtada' muqaddar) to which *ilā* is attached, and the estimate is: "Is there in you a desire, or is there in you an inclination, or is there in you a path to purification?" Similar to this is the saying of people: *hal laka fi al-khayr?* ("Is there for you in goodness?") meaning: "Is there for you a desire for goodness?" From this is the saying of the poet:

؎ فَهَلْ لَكَمَ فِيها إلَيَّ فَإنَّنِي ∗∗∗ بَصِيرٌ بِما أعْيا النِّطاسِيَّ جَذِيمًا

"Then is there for you (to come) to me in this matter? Indeed I am skilled in what baffled the physician Jadhīm."

﴿وأهْدِيَكَ إلى رَبِّكَ فَتَخْشى﴾ ("and I would guide you to your Lord, so you would fear Him") — that is, I would guide you to His worship and His unity, so that you would fear His punishment. The *fā'* (so) indicates the sequence of fear upon guidance, because fear cannot be except from one who is guided and rightly guided.

﴿فَأراهُ الآيَةَ الكُبْرى﴾ ("Then he showed him the greatest sign") — this *fā'* is the *fā' faṣīḥah* (the eloquent *fā'*), because it reveals an omitted speech. The meaning is: so he went and said to him what he said, as Allah related in more than one place, and he (Pharaoh) answered him with what he answered, until he said ﴿إنْ كُنْتَ جِئْتَ بِآيَةٍ فَأْتِ بِها﴾ ("If you have come with a sign, then produce it") [al-A'raf: 106]. At that point he showed him the greatest sign.

They differed regarding what the greatest sign was. It was said: the staff; it was said: his hand; it was said: the splitting of the sea; and it was said: it is all of the nine signs he brought.

﴿فَكَذَّبَ وعَصى﴾ ("But he denied and disobeyed") — that is, when he showed him the greatest sign, he denied Moses and what he brought and disobeyed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so he did not obey Him.

﴿ثُمَّ أدْبَرَ﴾ ("Then he turned his back") — that is, he turned away and withdrew from faith. ﴿يَسْعى﴾ ("striving") — that is, he worked at corruption upon the earth and strove to oppose what Moses brought. It was also said: *adbara* means he fled from the serpent, hastening out of fear of it.

Al-Razi said: the meaning of ﴿أدْبَرَ يَسْعى﴾ is "he came forward, hastening," just as one says *aqbala yaf'alu kadhā*, meaning "he began to do such-and-such." So *adbara* was put in the place of *aqbala* so that he would not be described as advancing.

﴿فَحَشَرَ﴾ ("Then he gathered") — that is, he gathered his troops for fighting and warfare, or gathered the magicians for opposition, or gathered the people to be present to witness what would happen, or gathered them so that they might protect him from the serpent.

﴿فَنادى فَقالَ أنا رَبُّكُمُ الأعْلى﴾ ("And he proclaimed, saying, 'I am your most exalted lord'") — that is, he said to them with a loud voice, or he ordered someone to proclaim this statement.

The meaning of ﴿أنا رَبُّكُمُ الأعْلى﴾ is that there is no lord above me.

ʻAṭāʼ said: he had made for them small idols and ordered them to worship them, and said: "I am the lord of your idols." It was also said that by his being their lord he meant that he was their leader and their master.

The first is preferable, because of His saying in another verse: ﴿ما عَلِمْتُ لَكم مِن إلَهٍ غَيْرِي﴾ ("I know of no god for you other than me") [al-Qasas: 38].

﴿فَأخَذَهُ اللَّهُ نَكالَ الآخِرَةِ والأُولى﴾ ("So Allah seized him, the punishment of the Hereafter and of this world") — *nakāl* is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun: that is, He seized him with a seizing of punishment; or it is a verbal noun of an omitted verb: that is, Allah seized him and made an example of him, the punishment of the Hereafter and the first; or it is an emphatic verbal noun for the content of the sentence. By "the punishment of the Hereafter" is meant the torment of the Fire, and "the punishment of the first" is the torment of this world by drowning.

Mujahid said: the torment of the beginning of his life and its end.

Qatadah said: the "Hereafter" is His saying ﴿أنا رَبُّكُمُ الأعْلى﴾, and the "first" is his denial of Moses.

It was also said: the "Hereafter" is His saying ﴿أنا رَبُّكُمُ الأعْلى﴾, and the first is His saying ﴿ما عَلِمْتُ لَكم مِن إلَهٍ غَيْرِي﴾. Between the two statements there were forty years.

It is permissible for *nakāla* to be in the accusative as an object of purpose (mafʻūl lahu): that is, Allah seized him for the sake of an example. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative by removing the preposition: that is, "with a punishment."

Al-Zajjaj preferred that it is an emphatic verbal noun, saying: because the meaning of "Allah seized him" is "Allah made an example of him with him," so it is derived from its meaning and not from its wording.

Al-Farra' said: that is, Allah seized him with a seizing of *nakāl*, i.e., for the sake of punishment. *Al-nakāl* is the name of what is made a punishment for others, i.e., a penalty for him. It is said *nakkala fulān bi-fulān* when he punished him.

The origin of the word is from restraint, and from it comes *al-nukūl ʻan al-yamīn* (refusing to take an oath), and *al-nakl* is a fetter.

﴿إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَعِبْرَةً لِمَن يَخْشى﴾ ("Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears") — that is, in what has been mentioned of the story of Pharaoh and what was done to him is a great lesson for one whose nature is to fear Allah and be mindful of Him, to fear His punishment and to beware of His anger.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʻAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib regarding His saying ﴿والنّازِعاتِ غَرْقًا﴾ ("By those who drag out with violence"): he said: they are the angels who draw out the souls of the disbelievers. ﴿والنّاشِطاتِ نَشْطًا﴾ ("and those who draw out gently"): he said: they are the angels who draw out the souls of the disbelievers from between the nails and the skin until they bring them out. ﴿والسّابِحاتِ سَبْحًا﴾ ("and those who glide swiftly"): they are the angels who glide with the souls of the believers between heaven and earth. ﴿فالسّابِقاتِ سَبْقًا﴾ ("then those who race forward"): they are the angels, some of whom outrace others with the souls of the believers to Allah. ﴿فالمُدَبِّراتِ أمْرًا﴾ ("then those who arrange affairs"): they are the angels who arrange the affairs of the servants from year to year.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʻAbbas regarding ﴿والنّازِعاتِ غَرْقًا﴾: he said: they are the souls of the disbelievers, which are drawn out, then drawn gently, then drowned in the Fire.

al-Hakim narrated and authenticated from him regarding ﴿والنّازِعاتِ غَرْقًا﴾ and ﴿والنّاشِطاتِ نَشْطًا﴾: he said: it is death.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿والنّازِعاتِ غَرْقًا﴾: he said: the angels who attend to the souls of the disbelievers. Up to His saying ﴿والسّابِحاتِ سَبْحًا﴾: he said: the angels.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Do not tear people apart, lest the dogs of the Fire tear you apart. Allah said: ﴿والناشِطاتِ نَشْطًا﴾. Do you know what it is?" I said: "O Prophet of Allah, what is it?" He said: "Dogs in the Fire that draw out flesh and bone."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʻAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib that Ibn al-Kawwa' asked him about ﴿فالمُدَبِّراتِ أمْرًا﴾, and he said: they are the angels who arrange the remembrance and command of the Most Merciful.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Dhikr al-Mawt* narrated from Ibn ʻAbbas, who said: ﴿فالمُدَبِّراتِ أمْرًا﴾: they are angels who are with the Angel of Death, attending the dead at the taking of their souls. Among them are those who raise up the soul, among them are those who say "Amen" to the supplication, and among them are those who ask forgiveness for the deceased until he is prayed over and lowered into his grave.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿يَوْمَ تَرْجُفُ الرّاجِفَةُ﴾ ("On the Day the quake will convulse"): he said: it is the first blast. ﴿تَتْبَعُها الرّادِفَةُ﴾ ("followed by the second"): he said: the second blast. ﴿قُلُوبٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ واجِفَةٌ﴾ ("Hearts that Day will be pounding"): he said: fearful. ﴿أئِنّا لَمَرْدُودُونَ في الحافِرَةِ﴾ ("Shall we indeed be returned to our former state?"): he said: life.

Ahmad, ʻAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it ḥasan), Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *Shuʻab al-Iman* narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "When a quarter of the night had passed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would rise and say: 'O people, remember Allah! The quake has come, followed by the second; death has come with what it carries.'"

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The earth will quake with a great quaking, and its inhabitants will be shaken. It is the one of which Allah says: ﴿يَوْمَ تَرْجُفُ الرّاجِفَةُ تَتْبَعُها الرّادِفَةُ﴾." He said: "Like a ship on the sea that tilts with its people, like a lamp suspended by its sides."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʻAbbas regarding ﴿قُلُوبٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ واجِفَةٌ﴾: he said: frightened and agitated.

ʻAbd ibn Humayd narrated from him regarding ﴿أئِنّا لَمَرْدُودُونَ في الحافِرَةِ﴾: he said: a new creation.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 79, verse 1–26 (part 3 of 3):

Abu 'Ubayd (d. 224 AH) in his Fada'il (Virtues of the Qur'an), Ibn al-Anbari in al-Waqf wa'l-Ibtida' (Stopping and Starting), 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim all narrated from him (Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him), also, that he was asked about the words of Allah: ﴿So they will be upon the surface of the earth﴾ and he said: "al-Sahirah is the surface of the earth." In another wording he said: "The whole earth is sahirah. Do you not see the saying of the poet:
"The game of the sea and the game of the sahirah"

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat also narrated from him, regarding the words ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ that he said: "Would you like to say: There is no god but Allah?"

Ibn Jarir also narrated from him regarding ﴿So Allah seized him in the punishment of the Hereafter and the former﴾ that he said: "It refers to his saying: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾, and the former (al-ula) refers to his saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas: 38]."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr that he said: "Between his two words there were forty years."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 79, verses 1–26 (part 1 of 3):

It is Meccan, without any disagreement.

Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Nazi'at was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Allah, glorified is He, swore by these things He mentioned, which are the angels who draw out the souls of the servants from their bodies, as one who draws a bow pulls it until he reaches its full extent. Likewise, what is meant by "al-nashitat" (those who unfasten), "al-sabihat" (those who glide) and "al-sabiqat" (those who outstrip) and "al-mudabbirat" (those who arrange affairs) is the angels. The conjunction (of these descriptions) with the unity of the referent is to treat the difference in attributes as if it were a difference in essence, as in the words of the poet:

"To the stern king, and the son of the brave hero, and the lion of the battalion in the crowded press."

This is the view of the majority of the Companions (Sahabah), the Successors (Tabi'un) and those after them.

al-Suddi said: "al-Nazi'at are the souls when they sink into the chests."

Mujahid said: "They are death, drawing out the soul."

Qatadah said: "They are the stars that draw from one horizon to another, from the saying 'nazaʻa ilayhi' (he went toward it) when he departed, or from the saying 'nazaʻat bil-habl' (she pulled with the rope), meaning that they set, disappear and rise from another horizon."

Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Akhfash and Ibn Kaysan held the same view.

'Ata' and 'Ikrimah said: "al-Nazi'at are the bows which draw the arrows. The extreme drawing of the one who draws the bow is that he pulls it to its full extent until it reaches the arrowhead."

Yahya ibn Salam said: "They draw (the animals) between the pastures and make them flee." It was also said that by al-Nazi'at he meant the raiding archers.

The accusative of "gharqan" is that it is a verbal noun (masdar) with its extra letters omitted, meaning "ighraqan" (extreme). Its governing verb is what precedes it, because it corresponds to it in meaning, meaning: extremity in drawing, in that they draw them from the farthest parts of the bodies. Or it is in the accusative of state, meaning: possessing extremity. It is said "aghraqa fi al-shay'" (he went to the extreme in the matter) when one goes deep into it and reaches its utmost limit.

The meaning of "wal-nashitat" is that they unfasten the souls, meaning they bring them out of the bodies, as a tether is unfastened from the foot of a camel when it is untied. It is said "nashaṭa al-rajul al-dalw min al-bi'r" (the man drew the bucket out of the well) when he brought it out. And "al-nashat" is pulling swiftly, and from it comes "al-unshuta" (the slip-knot), the knot which is easy to undo.

Abu Zayd said: "nashatu al-habl, anshuṭuhu, nashaṭan" means I tied it, and "anshaṭtuhu" means I untied it, and "anshaṭtu al-habl" means I stretched the rope.

al-Farra' said: "ansha al-'iqal" means it untied, and "nashiṭa" means he tied the rope on his hands.

al-Asma'i said: "Bi'r anshat" is a well whose bottom is near, from which the bucket comes out with a single pull, and "bi'r nashut" is one from which the bucket does not come out until it is pulled hard many times.

Mujahid said: "It is death, which unfastens the soul of the human being."

al-Suddi said: "They are the souls when they are unfastened from the two feet."

'Ikrimah and 'Ata' said: "They are the nooses that release the arrows." Qatadah, al-Hasan and al-Akhfash said: "They are the stars that move from one horizon to another, meaning they go away."

In al-Sihah it is said: "wal-nashitat nashtan" means the stars from one constellation to another, "like the unbridled bull from one land to another," and "the worries move their owner."

Abu 'Ubaydah and Qatadah said: "They are the wild beasts when they move from one land to another."

It was also said: "al-Nashitat" refers to the souls of the believers, and "al-Nazi'at" refers to the souls of the disbelievers, because the angel draws the soul of the believer gently and draws the soul of the disbeliever violently. His saying "nashtan" is a verbal noun, and likewise "sabhan" and "sabqan."

"Al-Sabihat" are the angels who swim in the bodies to bring out the soul, as the diver swims in the sea to bring out something from it.

Mujahid and Abu Salih said: "They are the angels who descend from the sky hastening by the command of Allah, as one says of a noble horse, 'sabih,' when it hastens in its running."

Mujahid also said: "al-Sabihat: death, which swims in the souls of the children of Adam."

It was also said: "They are the horses swimming in the raid." From this is the saying of 'Antarah:

"And the horses know, when they swim (sabh) into the cisterns of death, a swim."

Qatadah and al-Hasan said: "They are the stars which swim in their orbits, as in His saying: ﴿And each in an orbit they swim﴾ [Ya-Sin: 40]." 'Ata' said: "They are the ships which swim on the water." It was also said: "They are the spirits of the believers which swim out of longing for Allah."

﴿Then those who outstrip, outstripping﴾: they are the angels according to the view of the majority, as has passed.

Masruq and Mujahid said: "The angels outstrip the devils to the prophets with the revelation."

Abu Rawq said: "They are the angels who precede the son of Adam with good and righteous deeds." Something similar was narrated from Mujahid.

Muqatil said: "They precede with the souls of the believers to Paradise."

al-Rabi' said: "They are the souls of the believers which outstrip to the angels out of longing for Allah."

Mujahid also said: "It is death, which outstrips the human being."

Qatadah, al-Hasan and Ma'mar said: "They are the stars, some of which outstrip others in their course."

'Ata' said: "They are the horses which outstrip to the jihad."

It was also said: "They are the spirits which precede the bodies to Paradise or to the Fire."

al-Jurjani said: "He connected 'al-sabiqat' with the letter fa' because they are causes of what came before them, meaning: if you said 'he stood and went' with the letter wa', the standing would not have been a cause of the going."

al-Wahidi said: "This is not consistent in His saying: ﴿Then those who arrange affairs, arranging﴾, because it is far-fetched to make the outstripping a cause of arranging."

al-Razi said: "The answer to what al-Wahidi said is that when they were commanded, they swam, then they outstripped, then they arranged what they were commanded to arrange, so these are acts that are connected to one another, like the saying: 'Zayd stood up and then went.' When they outstripped in acts of obedience and hastened to them, their trustworthiness became apparent, so the arranging was entrusted to them."

It is answered that outstripping is not a cause of arranging, just as swimming is not a cause of outstripping and standing is not a cause of going. Mere connection does not necessitate causation and being caused.

The better view is that the conjunction with fa' in "al-mudabbirat" is made to correspond to the conjunction with fa' before it, "al-sabiqat," and it does not need a special reason as the earlier one did, because a special reason is sought only for the later differing from the earlier, not for its agreement and conformity with it.

﴿Then those who arrange affairs, arranging﴾: al-Qushayri said: "They agreed that what is meant here is the angels."

al-Mawardi said: "There are two views on this: the first is that they are the angels, which is the view of the majority. The second is that they are the seven planets, reported by Khalid ibn Ma'dan from Mu'adh ibn Jabal."

Regarding their arranging the affair, there are two views: the first is that they arrange the rising and setting of the stars. The second is arranging what Allah decreed in them of states.

The meaning of the angels' arranging the affair is their descent with the lawful and the unlawful and their detailing of them. Although the true agent of arranging is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, when the angels descended with it, it was attributed to them.

It was also said that when the angels were commanded to arrange the affairs of the people of the earth concerning winds, rains and other things, they were called "mudabbirat."

'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabat said: "The arranging of the affairs of this world is entrusted to four angels: Jibril, Mika'il, 'Izra'il and Israfil. As for Jibril, he is in charge of the winds and the armies. As for Mika'il, he is in charge of rain and plants. As for 'Izra'il, he is in charge of seizing the souls. As for Israfil, he descends with the command to them."

The answer to the oath by these matters, which Allah swore by, is omitted; the meaning is: "By the drawers, and likewise, and likewise, you will surely be raised."

al-Farra' said: "It is omitted because the listeners know it, and His saying indicates it: ﴿Shall we, when we are bones decayed?﴾"

It was also said that the answer to the oath is His saying: ﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾, meaning: indeed in the Day of Resurrection and the mention of Musa and Fir'awn there is a lesson for whoever fears.

Ibn al-Anbari said: "This is ugly, because the speech has been lengthy between them."

It was also said that the answer to the oath is: ﴿Has there come to you the report of Musa?﴾, because the meaning is "it has come to you." This is very weak.

It was also said that the answer is: ﴿On the Day the quaking one quakes﴾, on the assumption of: "On the Day the quaking one quakes, the following one follows."

al-Sijistani said: "It is possible that this is of inversion, as if He said: 'Then they are in the awakened place, and by the drawers.'"

Ibn al-Anbari said: "This is an error, because the fa' is not used to begin speech. The first view is better."

﴿On the Day the quaking one quakes﴾: the accusative of this time expression is by the omitted answer to the oath, or by the implied verb "remember." Al-Rajifah means the one that trembles; it is said "rajafa yarjufu" when it trembles. Here it means the great cry in which there is shaking and agitation like thunder, and it is the first blast by which all creatures die. Al-Radifah is the second blast, which occurs at the resurrection, and it was called "radifah" because it follows the first blast. This is what the majority of the exegetes said.

Ibn Zayd said: "al-Rajifah is the earth, and al-Radifah is the Hour."

Mujahid said: "al-Radifah is the earthquake, and the following one is the cry." It was also said: "al-Rajifah is the trembling of the earth and al-Radifah is the earthquake." The root of "rajfah" is movement, and the meaning is not merely movement here. Rather, al-Rajifah here is derived from the saying: "rajafa al-ra'd yarjufu rajfan wa rajifan" when the sound of the thunder appears. From this came "al-arajif" (rumours), because of the agitation of voices in them and the appearance of voices in them. From this is the saying of the poet:

"With rumours, O son of baseness, you threaten me, and in rumours I thought baseness and weakness."

The position of "tatba'uha al-radifah" (the following one follows it) is accusative as a state of "al-rajifah," and the meaning: you will surely be raised on the day of the first blast, in the state that the second blast follows it.

﴿Hearts on that Day will be trembling﴾: "qulub" is the subject, "yawma'idhin" is in the accusative governed by "wajifah," and "wajifah" is an adjective of "qulub."

The sentence ﴿their eyes will be humbled﴾ is the predicate of "qulub." al-Rajifah means agitated and restless, because of what they witnessed of the horrors of the Day of Resurrection.

The majority of the exegetes said: "That is, afraid and fearful."

al-Suddi said: "Removed from their places," similar to ﴿When hearts reach the throats﴾ [Ghafir: 18]. al-Mu'arrij said: "Restless, anxious."

al-Mubarrad said: "Agitated. It is said 'wajafa al-qalb yajifu wajifan' when it pounds, as one says 'wajaba yajibu wajiban.' The 'ijaf' is swift travel, so the root of 'wajif' is agitation of the heart."

From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Khatim:

"Indeed the sons of Jahjaba and their people, our livers behind them tremble."

"Their eyes will be humbled": that is, the eyes of its owners, so the possessive was omitted. "Khashi'ah" means humiliated, and what is meant is that humiliation and submission appear upon them at witnessing the horrors of the Day of Resurrection, like His saying: ﴿Humbled from humiliation﴾ [al-Shura: 45].

'Ata' said: "He means the eyes of those who died without Islam, and the context indicates this, since the context concerns those who deny resurrection."

﴿They say: "Shall we indeed be returned to the former state?"﴾: this is a report of what the deniers of resurrection say when they are told that they will be raised. That is: shall we be returned to our first condition and the beginning of our affair, so that we become alive after our death? It is said "raja'a fulan fi hafiratih," meaning he returned from where he came. al-Hafirah, among the Arabs, is the name for the beginning of a thing and the start of an affair. From this is the saying: "raja'a fulan 'ala hafiratih," meaning on the road by which he came. It is also said: "They fought at the hafirah," meaning at the first meeting. The road by which one came is called "hafirah" because of its being impressed upon it by his walking on it, so it is "hafirah" in the sense of "mahfurah" (dug out). From this is the saying of the poet:

"Shall I return on a bald head and white hair? God forbid from folly and shame."

Meaning: shall I return to what I was in my youth of amorous pursuit after white hair and baldness? It was said: "al-Hafirah" is "al-'ajilah" (the present life), and the meaning is: indeed we will be returned to the world. It was said: "al-Hafirah" is the earth in which their graves are dug. From this is the saying of the poet:

"I swore I would not forget you, so know, until people are returned to the hafirah."

The meaning: indeed we will be returned in our graves alive. So said al-Khalil and al-Farra', and Mujahid said likewise.

Ibn Zayd said: "al-Hafirah is the Fire," and he took as evidence His saying: ﴿That, then, would be a losing return﴾.

al-Jumhur read ﴿fi al-hafirah﴾, and Abu Haywah read "fi al-hufrah" (in the pit).

﴿Shall we, when we are bones decayed?﴾: that is, crumbling and disintegrating. It is said "nakhira al-'azm" (the bone decayed) when it deteriorates. This is an emphasis on the denial of resurrection: that is, how can we be returned alive and raised when we are decayed bones? The governing element in "idha" is implied, indicated by "mardudun": that is, shall we, when we are decayed bones, be returned and raised, while being the thing farthest from life?

The commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on Surah 79, verses 1–26 (part 2 of 3):

The majority (al-Jumhur) read *nakhirah* (نَخِرَةً). Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr read *nakhirah* with an alif (ناخِرَةً). Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred the first reading, while al-Farra', Ibn Jarir and Abu Mu'adh al-Nahwi preferred the second.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: *al-nakhirah* is the bone that has not yet been hollowed out (lam tunkhar ba'd), meaning it has not yet decayed, though it will inevitably be hollowed out.

It was also said that the two forms have the same meaning. The Arabs say *nakhira al-shay'* so it is *nākhir* and *nakhir*, and *ṭami'a* so it is *ṭāmi'* and *ṭami'*, and similar forms.

Al-Akhfash said: both are dialectal variants (lughatān), and whichever you recite is good.

The poet said:

؎ يَظَلُّ بِها الشَّيْخُ الَّذِي كانَ بادِنًا ∗∗∗ يَدُبُّ عَلى عِوَجٍ لَهُ نَخِراتُ

"The old man who was once corpulent crawls upon it, on crooked limbs that are hollowed out (nakhirāt)."

He means: on crooked legs.

It was also said that *al-nākhirah* is the bone whose extremities have been eaten away while its middle remains, and *al-nakhirah* is the bone that has entirely decayed.

Mujahid said: *nakhirah* means *marfūtah* (crumbled to dust), as in His saying ﴿رُفاتًا﴾ (dust). It has also been recited as ﴿إذا كُنّا﴾ and as ﴿أئِذا كُنّا﴾, with the interrogative and without it.

Then Allah, glorified is He, related another statement of theirs, saying: ﴿They said, "That would then be a losing return."﴾ That is, a return that brings loss to those who experience it. The meaning is that they said: if we are returned after death, we will surely suffer loss through what will befall us after death from what Muhammad says.

It was also said that the meaning of *khāsirah* is *kādhibah* (false), i.e., it will not come to pass. This is what al-Hasan and others said.

Al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: *khāsirah* means losing for the one who denies it.

Qatadah and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: that is, if we are returned after death, we will surely lose through the Fire. They only said this because they had been threatened with the Fire. *Al-karrah* means the return, and its plural is *karrāt*.

His saying ﴿فَإنَّما هي زَجْرَةٌ واحِدَةٌ﴾ ("It will be but a single blast") is a justification for what precedes it, namely their disbelief in the resurrection of the decayed bones and the revival of the dead. The meaning is: do not regard that as unlikely, for it will be but a single blast, and that will be the revival and resurrection. By *zajrah* is meant the cry (al-ṣayḥah), which is the second blast by which resurrection occurs.

It was also said that the pronoun in His saying ﴿إنَّما هي﴾ refers to *al-rādifah* mentioned earlier.

﴿فَإذا هم بِالسّاهِرَةِ﴾ ("then they will be on the surface of the earth"), that is, then the creatures who had died and been buried will be alive upon the face of the earth. Al-Wahidi said: by *al-sāhirah* is meant the face of the earth and its surface, according to the consensus.

Al-Farra' said: it was called this name because on it is the sleep and wakefulness of living creatures. It was also said that it is called this because a person stays awake in its deserts out of fear of it. From this is the saying of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali:

؎ يَرُدُّونَ ساهِرَةً كَأنَّ حَمِيمَها ∗∗∗ وغَمِيمَها أسْدافُ لَيْلٍ مُظْلِمِ

"They pass through a sāhirah whose depths and whose surface are like the dark mantles of a gloomy night."

And the saying of Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt:

؎ وفِيها لَحْمُ ساهِرَةٍ وبَحْرٌ ∗∗∗ وما فاهُوا بِهِ لَهُمُ مُقِيمُ

"In it is the flesh of the sāhirah and the sea, and what they utter remains with them."

He means the flesh of the living creatures of the sāhirah land.

In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* it says: *al-sāhirah* is the face of the earth, and from this is His saying ﴿فَإذا هم بِالسّاهِرَةِ﴾.

It also says: *al-sāhirah* is a white land. It was said it is a land of silver upon which Allah, glorified is He, was never disobeyed. It was also said that *al-sāhirah* is the seventh earth, which Allah, glorified is He, will bring forth, and upon it He will call the creatures to account.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: *al-sāhirah* is the land of Syria.

Qatadah said: it is Hell (jahannam). That is: then these disbelievers will be in Hell. It is called *sāhirah* because they do not sleep in it, due to the continuity of their punishment.

The sentence ﴿هَلْ أتاكَ حَدِيثُ مُوسى﴾ ("Has there reached you the story of Moses?") is a new sentence (mustaʼnafah), brought to console the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding the denial of his people, and that there will befall them the like of what befell those before them who were stronger than them. The meaning of *hal atāka* is: "has there come to you and reached you?" This is on the assumption that he had heard of the stories of Pharaoh and Moses that would make him know their account. On the other assumption, that this was the first revelation to him concerning them, the meaning is interrogative: "Has there come to you the story of him? I will inform you of it."

﴿إذْ ناداهُ رَبُّهُ بِالوادِي المُقَدَّسِ طُوًى﴾ ("when his Lord called to him in the sacred valley of Tuwa") — the adverbial phrase is attached to *ḥadīth* (the story), not to *atāka* (has come), because their times differ. The story of Moses and Pharaoh has already passed in more than one place, where there is sufficiency. The difference among the readers regarding *Ṭuwā* has already been mentioned in Surah Ṭā-Hā.

*Al-wādī al-muqaddas* means the blessed and purified valley.

Al-Farra' said: *Ṭuwā* is a valley between Medina and Egypt. He said: it is a *maʻdūl* (a word altered from its original form) from *ṭāwin*, just as ʻUmar is altered from ʻĀmir. He said: *al-ṣarf* (declension with tanwin) is more beloved to me, since I have not found a parallel to this altered form.

It was also said that *Ṭuwā* means "O man" in Hebrew, so it is as if it were said: "O man, go!" It was also said that the meaning is: the sacred valley was blessed twice, and the first meaning is preferable.

The detailed discussion of this has already passed.

﴿اذْهَبْ إلى فِرْعَوْنَ إنَّهُ طَغى﴾ ("Go to Pharaoh; indeed he has transgressed") — it was said this is under an implied *qawl* (saying), and it was said it is an explanation of the calling: that is, He called him with a call which is His saying "Go." It was also said it is under the omission of the explanatory *an* (أنْ), and this is supported by Ibn Mas'ud's reading ﴿أنِ اذْهَبْ﴾, because a call carries the meaning of saying. The clause ﴿إنَّهُ طَغى﴾ ("indeed he has transgressed") is a justification for the command, or for the obligation of obedience: that is, he exceeded the limit in disobedience, arrogance and disbelief in Allah.

Then say to him ﴿هَلْ لَكَ إلى أنْ تَزَكّى﴾ ("Would you like to purify yourself?"), that is, His saying, after your arrival to him: is there in you a desire for purification (tazakkī), which is cleansing oneself from polytheism. Its original form is *tatazakkā*, and one of the two *tā'* was deleted.

The majority read *tazakkā* with a light (takhfif) pronunciation. Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read it with the *zāy* doubled, through assimilating the *tā'* into the *zāy*.

Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: the meaning of the light reading is "that you become pure and believing," and the meaning of the doubled reading is "giving charity (ṣadaqah)." In the sentence there is an implied subject (mubtada' muqaddar) to which *ilā* is attached, and the estimate is: "Is there in you a desire, or is there in you an inclination, or is there in you a path to purification?" Similar to this is the saying of people: *hal laka fi al-khayr?* ("Is there for you in goodness?") meaning: "Is there for you a desire for goodness?" From this is the saying of the poet:

؎ فَهَلْ لَكَمَ فِيها إلَيَّ فَإنَّنِي ∗∗∗ بَصِيرٌ بِما أعْيا النِّطاسِيَّ جَذِيمًا

"Then is there for you (to come) to me in this matter? Indeed I am skilled in what baffled the physician Jadhīm."

﴿وأهْدِيَكَ إلى رَبِّكَ فَتَخْشى﴾ ("and I would guide you to your Lord, so you would fear Him") — that is, I would guide you to His worship and His unity, so that you would fear His punishment. The *fā'* (so) indicates the sequence of fear upon guidance, because fear cannot be except from one who is guided and rightly guided.

﴿فَأراهُ الآيَةَ الكُبْرى﴾ ("Then he showed him the greatest sign") — this *fā'* is the *fā' faṣīḥah* (the eloquent *fā'*), because it reveals an omitted speech. The meaning is: so he went and said to him what he said, as Allah related in more than one place, and he (Pharaoh) answered him with what he answered, until he said ﴿إنْ كُنْتَ جِئْتَ بِآيَةٍ فَأْتِ بِها﴾ ("If you have come with a sign, then produce it") [al-A'raf: 106]. At that point he showed him the greatest sign.

They differed regarding what the greatest sign was. It was said: the staff; it was said: his hand; it was said: the splitting of the sea; and it was said: it is all of the nine signs he brought.

﴿فَكَذَّبَ وعَصى﴾ ("But he denied and disobeyed") — that is, when he showed him the greatest sign, he denied Moses and what he brought and disobeyed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, so he did not obey Him.

﴿ثُمَّ أدْبَرَ﴾ ("Then he turned his back") — that is, he turned away and withdrew from faith. ﴿يَسْعى﴾ ("striving") — that is, he worked at corruption upon the earth and strove to oppose what Moses brought. It was also said: *adbara* means he fled from the serpent, hastening out of fear of it.

Al-Razi said: the meaning of ﴿أدْبَرَ يَسْعى﴾ is "he came forward, hastening," just as one says *aqbala yaf'alu kadhā*, meaning "he began to do such-and-such." So *adbara* was put in the place of *aqbala* so that he would not be described as advancing.

﴿فَحَشَرَ﴾ ("Then he gathered") — that is, he gathered his troops for fighting and warfare, or gathered the magicians for opposition, or gathered the people to be present to witness what would happen, or gathered them so that they might protect him from the serpent.

﴿فَنادى فَقالَ أنا رَبُّكُمُ الأعْلى﴾ ("And he proclaimed, saying, 'I am your most exalted lord'") — that is, he said to them with a loud voice, or he ordered someone to proclaim this statement.

The meaning of ﴿أنا رَبُّكُمُ الأعْلى﴾ is that there is no lord above me.

ʻAṭāʼ said: he had made for them small idols and ordered them to worship them, and said: "I am the lord of your idols." It was also said that by his being their lord he meant that he was their leader and their master.

The first is preferable, because of His saying in another verse: ﴿ما عَلِمْتُ لَكم مِن إلَهٍ غَيْرِي﴾ ("I know of no god for you other than me") [al-Qasas: 38].

﴿فَأخَذَهُ اللَّهُ نَكالَ الآخِرَةِ والأُولى﴾ ("So Allah seized him, the punishment of the Hereafter and of this world") — *nakāl* is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun: that is, He seized him with a seizing of punishment; or it is a verbal noun of an omitted verb: that is, Allah seized him and made an example of him, the punishment of the Hereafter and the first; or it is an emphatic verbal noun for the content of the sentence. By "the punishment of the Hereafter" is meant the torment of the Fire, and "the punishment of the first" is the torment of this world by drowning.

Mujahid said: the torment of the beginning of his life and its end.

Qatadah said: the "Hereafter" is His saying ﴿أنا رَبُّكُمُ الأعْلى﴾, and the "first" is his denial of Moses.

It was also said: the "Hereafter" is His saying ﴿أنا رَبُّكُمُ الأعْلى﴾, and the first is His saying ﴿ما عَلِمْتُ لَكم مِن إلَهٍ غَيْرِي﴾. Between the two statements there were forty years.

It is permissible for *nakāla* to be in the accusative as an object of purpose (mafʻūl lahu): that is, Allah seized him for the sake of an example. It is also permissible for it to be in the accusative by removing the preposition: that is, "with a punishment."

Al-Zajjaj preferred that it is an emphatic verbal noun, saying: because the meaning of "Allah seized him" is "Allah made an example of him with him," so it is derived from its meaning and not from its wording.

Al-Farra' said: that is, Allah seized him with a seizing of *nakāl*, i.e., for the sake of punishment. *Al-nakāl* is the name of what is made a punishment for others, i.e., a penalty for him. It is said *nakkala fulān bi-fulān* when he punished him.

The origin of the word is from restraint, and from it comes *al-nukūl ʻan al-yamīn* (refusing to take an oath), and *al-nakl* is a fetter.

﴿إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَعِبْرَةً لِمَن يَخْشى﴾ ("Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears") — that is, in what has been mentioned of the story of Pharaoh and what was done to him is a great lesson for one whose nature is to fear Allah and be mindful of Him, to fear His punishment and to beware of His anger.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from ʻAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib regarding His saying ﴿والنّازِعاتِ غَرْقًا﴾ ("By those who drag out with violence"): he said: they are the angels who draw out the souls of the disbelievers. ﴿والنّاشِطاتِ نَشْطًا﴾ ("and those who draw out gently"): he said: they are the angels who draw out the souls of the disbelievers from between the nails and the skin until they bring them out. ﴿والسّابِحاتِ سَبْحًا﴾ ("and those who glide swiftly"): they are the angels who glide with the souls of the believers between heaven and earth. ﴿فالسّابِقاتِ سَبْقًا﴾ ("then those who race forward"): they are the angels, some of whom outrace others with the souls of the believers to Allah. ﴿فالمُدَبِّراتِ أمْرًا﴾ ("then those who arrange affairs"): they are the angels who arrange the affairs of the servants from year to year.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn ʻAbbas regarding ﴿والنّازِعاتِ غَرْقًا﴾: he said: they are the souls of the disbelievers, which are drawn out, then drawn gently, then drowned in the Fire.

al-Hakim narrated and authenticated from him regarding ﴿والنّازِعاتِ غَرْقًا﴾ and ﴿والنّاشِطاتِ نَشْطًا﴾: he said: it is death.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Mas'ud regarding ﴿والنّازِعاتِ غَرْقًا﴾: he said: the angels who attend to the souls of the disbelievers. Up to His saying ﴿والسّابِحاتِ سَبْحًا﴾: he said: the angels.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: "Do not tear people apart, lest the dogs of the Fire tear you apart. Allah said: ﴿والناشِطاتِ نَشْطًا﴾. Do you know what it is?" I said: "O Prophet of Allah, what is it?" He said: "Dogs in the Fire that draw out flesh and bone."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from ʻAlī ibn Abi Ṭālib that Ibn al-Kawwa' asked him about ﴿فالمُدَبِّراتِ أمْرًا﴾, and he said: they are the angels who arrange the remembrance and command of the Most Merciful.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Dhikr al-Mawt* narrated from Ibn ʻAbbas, who said: ﴿فالمُدَبِّراتِ أمْرًا﴾: they are angels who are with the Angel of Death, attending the dead at the taking of their souls. Among them are those who raise up the soul, among them are those who say "Amen" to the supplication, and among them are those who ask forgiveness for the deceased until he is prayed over and lowered into his grave.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding ﴿يَوْمَ تَرْجُفُ الرّاجِفَةُ﴾ ("On the Day the quake will convulse"): he said: it is the first blast. ﴿تَتْبَعُها الرّادِفَةُ﴾ ("followed by the second"): he said: the second blast. ﴿قُلُوبٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ واجِفَةٌ﴾ ("Hearts that Day will be pounding"): he said: fearful. ﴿أئِنّا لَمَرْدُودُونَ في الحافِرَةِ﴾ ("Shall we indeed be returned to our former state?"): he said: life.

Ahmad, ʻAbd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it ḥasan), Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *Shuʻab al-Iman* narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: "When a quarter of the night had passed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would rise and say: 'O people, remember Allah! The quake has come, followed by the second; death has come with what it carries.'"

Abu al-Shaykh, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The earth will quake with a great quaking, and its inhabitants will be shaken. It is the one of which Allah says: ﴿يَوْمَ تَرْجُفُ الرّاجِفَةُ تَتْبَعُها الرّادِفَةُ﴾." He said: "Like a ship on the sea that tilts with its people, like a lamp suspended by its sides."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʻAbbas regarding ﴿قُلُوبٌ يَوْمَئِذٍ واجِفَةٌ﴾: he said: frightened and agitated.

ʻAbd ibn Humayd narrated from him regarding ﴿أئِنّا لَمَرْدُودُونَ في الحافِرَةِ﴾: he said: a new creation.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 79, verse 1–26 (part 3 of 3):

Abu 'Ubayd (d. 224 AH) in his Fada'il (Virtues of the Qur'an), Ibn al-Anbari in al-Waqf wa'l-Ibtida' (Stopping and Starting), 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim all narrated from him (Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him), also, that he was asked about the words of Allah: ﴿So they will be upon the surface of the earth﴾ and he said: "al-Sahirah is the surface of the earth." In another wording he said: "The whole earth is sahirah. Do you not see the saying of the poet:
"The game of the sea and the game of the sahirah"

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat also narrated from him, regarding the words ﴿Would you like to purify yourself?﴾ that he said: "Would you like to say: There is no god but Allah?"

Ibn Jarir also narrated from him regarding ﴿So Allah seized him in the punishment of the Hereafter and the former﴾ that he said: "It refers to his saying: ﴿I am your lord, the Most High﴾, and the former (al-ula) refers to his saying: ﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas: 38]."

'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr that he said: "Between his two words there were forty years."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 79, verses 1–26 (part 1 of 3):

It is Meccan, without any disagreement.

Ibn al-Duraysi, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Surat al-Nazi'at was revealed in Mecca."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn al-Zubayr something similar.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Allah, glorified is He, swore by these things He mentioned, which are the angels who draw out the souls of the servants from their bodies, as one who draws a bow pulls it until he reaches its full extent. Likewise, what is meant by "al-nashitat" (those who unfasten), "al-sabihat" (those who glide) and "al-sabiqat" (those who outstrip) and "al-mudabbirat" (those who arrange affairs) is the angels. The conjunction (of these descriptions) with the unity of the referent is to treat the difference in attributes as if it were a difference in essence, as in the words of the poet:

"To the stern king, and the son of the brave hero, and the lion of the battalion in the crowded press."

This is the view of the majority of the Companions (Sahabah), the Successors (Tabi'un) and those after them.

al-Suddi said: "al-Nazi'at are the souls when they sink into the chests."

Mujahid said: "They are death, drawing out the soul."

Qatadah said: "They are the stars that draw from one horizon to another, from the saying 'nazaʻa ilayhi' (he went toward it) when he departed, or from the saying 'nazaʻat bil-habl' (she pulled with the rope), meaning that they set, disappear and rise from another horizon."

Abu 'Ubaydah, al-Akhfash and Ibn Kaysan held the same view.

'Ata' and 'Ikrimah said: "al-Nazi'at are the bows which draw the arrows. The extreme drawing of the one who draws the bow is that he pulls it to its full extent until it reaches the arrowhead."

Yahya ibn Salam said: "They draw (the animals) between the pastures and make them flee." It was also said that by al-Nazi'at he meant the raiding archers.

The accusative of "gharqan" is that it is a verbal noun (masdar) with its extra letters omitted, meaning "ighraqan" (extreme). Its governing verb is what precedes it, because it corresponds to it in meaning, meaning: extremity in drawing, in that they draw them from the farthest parts of the bodies.
