As for the response of "idha", it was said that it is His saying: ﴿Then as for he who transgressed﴾; and it was said that it is omitted, meaning: then the matter is so, or they witness it, or they know it, or the people of the Fire are made to enter the Fire and the people of Paradise enter Paradise.

Abu al-Baqa' said: its governing element is its response, which is the meaning of ﴿the Day when man will remember what he strove﴾, for it is in the accusative by a hidden verb: that is, "I mean the day when he remembers", or "the day when he remembers, such and such will be the case." It was also said that the adverbial phrase is a substitute for "idha", and it was said it is a substitute for "al-Tammah al-Kubra". The meaning of "man remembers what he strove" is that he remembers what he did of good or evil, because he sees it recorded in the pages of his deeds; and "ma" is either a verbal source or a relative pronoun.

﴿And Hellfire is brought forth for whoever sees﴾: it is conjoined to "jaat" (came). The meaning of "burrizat" is: it is made manifest, a manifestation that is hidden from no one.

Muqatil said: its covering is removed and the creatures look at it. It was also said: for whoever sees among the disbelievers, not among the believers. The apparent meaning is that it is displayed to every beholder; as for the believer, by seeing it he recognizes the extent of God's blessing upon him in being safe from it, and as for the disbeliever, his grief increases upon his grief and his regret upon his regret.

The majority read "li-man yara" with the verb in the third person masculine (yā'), while 'A'isha, Malik ibn Dinar, 'Ikrimah and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with the second person (tā'): that is, Hellfire is made to see whoever it sees, or it is made to see you, O Muhammad.

Ibn Mas'ud read "li-man ra'a" in the past tense form of the verb.

﴿As for him who transgressed﴾: that is, exceeded the limit in disbelief and sins.

﴿And preferred the worldly life﴾: that is, he put it ahead of the Hereafter, did not prepare for it, and did not do its deeds. ﴿Then indeed Hellfire is his refuge﴾: that is, his abode, and the alif and lam are a substitute for the genitive complement. The meaning is: it is his dwelling where he settles, and his refuge to which he returns, and nothing else.

Then He mentioned the second of the two divisions, saying: ﴿But as for he who feared the position of his Lord﴾: that is, he was wary of standing before his Lord on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Rabi' said: the position of the Day of Reckoning.

Qatadah said: He says that God, mighty and majestic, has a position which the believers fear.

Mujahid said: it is his fear in this world of God, mighty and majestic, when he is about to commit a sin, so he desists from it. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And for him who fears the position of his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46]. The first is more preferable. ﴿And restrained the soul from desire﴾: that is, he held it back from inclining toward sins and forbidden things that it desires.

Muqatil said: he is the man who intends a sin, then remembers his standing for reckoning, so he abandons it.

﴿Then indeed Paradise is his refuge﴾: that is, the abode where he settles, and the place to which he returns, and nothing else.

﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its arrival?﴾: that is, when its occurrence and establishment will be.

Al-Farra' said: that is, the end of its establishment, like the anchoring of a ship.

Abu 'Ubayda said: the anchorage (mursa) of a ship is when it comes to rest. The meaning is: they ask you about the Hour, when Allah will establish it. The explanation of this has already passed in Surah al-A'raf.

﴿In what are you concerned with its mention?﴾: that is, in what matter are you, O Muhammad, concerned with mentioning the Resurrection and asking about it? The meaning is: you are not in anything of its knowledge or its mention; only God, glorified is He, knows it. This is a denial and rejection of the polytheists' question about it: that is, in what are you about this, so that they ask you about it while you do not know it.

﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾: that is, the endpoint of its knowledge, so its knowledge is not found with anyone else. This is like His saying: ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 187] and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34]. So how could they ask you about it and seek from you a clarification of the time of its establishment?

﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾: that is, a warner to whoever fears the establishment of the Hour. That is your duty; there is nothing incumbent upon you beyond it, such as informing about the time of the Hour's establishment and similar matters that Allah has kept for Himself in knowledge. He restricted the warning to those who fear, because they are the ones who benefit from warning, although he is a warner to every accountable person, Muslim and disbeliever.

The majority read "mundhiru" with the genitive construction, annexing it to what follows. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Abu Ja'far, Talhah, Ibn Muhaysin, Shaybah, al-A'raj and Humayd read it with tanwin, and this reading is narrated from Abu 'Amr.

al-Farra' said: both tanwin and its omission in "mundhir" are correct, like His saying: ﴿Accomplishing His command﴾ [al-Talaq: 3] and ﴿Weakening the plot of the disbelievers﴾ [al-Anfal: 18].

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the annexation may be to the past tense, like "darib Zayd amsi" (the one who struck Zayd yesterday).

﴿As if they, on the day they see it, had not remained but an evening or its morning﴾: that is, only the amount of the end of a day or its beginning, or the amount of the forenoon that follows that evening. The intention is to minimize the duration of the worldly life, as He said: ﴿They will feel as if they had not remained but an hour of a day﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]. It was also said that they did not remain in their graves except an evening or its morning.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the intended meaning of annexing "duha" (forenoon) to "'ashiyyah" (evening) is its annexation to the day of the evening, according to the custom of the Arabs, who say: "I will come to you in the morning or its evening, and I will come to you in the evening or its morning", so that "al-'ashiyyah" means the end of the day and "al-ghadah" means the beginning of the day.

From this is the saying of the poet:

"We attacked 'Amir in its house, with swift horses racing through both ends of its day, in the evening of the crescent moon or its last phase."

The sentence confirms what the warning implies of the swiftness of the coming of what is warned of.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿He raised its height﴾, he said: He built it. ﴿And darkened its night﴾, he said: He made its night dark.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him: ﴿And darkened its night﴾, he said: and made its night dark. ﴿And brought forth its forenoon﴾, he said: He brought forth its daylight.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾, he said: "with that."

Ibn Ḥumayd (ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd) and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also transmitted from him (Ibn ʿAbbās) that a man said to him: "There are two verses in the Book of God that contradict each other." He said: "You have only been given this because of your own opinion." The man said: "Recite ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days…﴾ until ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 9–11], and His saying ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾." He said: "God created the earth before He created the heaven, and then He spread out the earth after He had created the heaven. And His saying daḥāhā means He spread it out (basaṭahā)."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim also transmitted from him: "Daḥāhā means that He brought forth from it water and pasture, split in it the rivers, and placed in it the mountains, the sands, the paths, the hills, and what lies between them, in two days."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also transmitted from him: "al-Ṭāmma is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to ask about the Hour, so this was revealed: ﴿In what are you about its mention?﴾"

al-Bazzār, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim (who declared it ṣaḥīḥ), and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from ʿĀʾisha, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) kept asking about the Hour until God revealed ﴿In what are you about its mention?﴾ ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾, and then he stopped and no longer asked about it."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ṭabarānī, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ṭāriq ibn Shihāb, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to mention the Hour frequently until ﴿In what are you about its mention?﴾ ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾ was revealed, and then he refrained from it."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās.

al-Suyūṭī said, with a weak chain: That is, the polytheists of Mecca asked the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "When is the Hour?", mocking him. So God revealed ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its arrival?﴾, meaning its coming, ﴿In what are you about its mention?﴾, meaning: what knowledge of it do you have, O Muḥammad, ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾, meaning the final limit of its knowledge.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from ʿĀʾisha, who said: "When the Bedouins (al-aʿrāb) came to the Prophet (ﷺ), they would ask him about the Hour, and he would look at the youngest person among them and say: 'If this one lives, your Hour will come upon you.'"

It was also said that the adverbial phrase is a substitute for "idha", and it was said it is a substitute for "al-Tammah al-Kubra". The meaning of "man remembers what he strove" is that he remembers what he did of good or evil, because he sees it recorded in the pages of his deeds; and "ma" is either a verbal source or a relative pronoun.

﴿And Hellfire is brought forth for whoever sees﴾: it is conjoined to "jaat" (came). The meaning of "burrizat" is: it is made manifest, a manifestation that is hidden from no one.

Muqatil said: its covering is removed and the creatures look at it. It was also said: for whoever sees among the disbelievers, not among the believers. The apparent meaning is that it is displayed to every beholder; as for the believer, by seeing it he recognizes the extent of God's blessing upon him in being safe from it, and as for the disbeliever, his grief increases upon his grief and his regret upon his regret.

The majority read "li-man yara" with the verb in the third person masculine (yā'), while 'A'isha, Malik ibn Dinar, 'Ikrimah and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with the second person (tā'): that is, Hellfire is made to see whoever it sees, or it is made to see you, O Muhammad.

Ibn Mas'ud read "li-man ra'a" in the past tense form of the verb.

﴿As for him who transgressed﴾: that is, exceeded the limit in disbelief and sins.

﴿And preferred the worldly life﴾: that is, he put it ahead of the Hereafter, did not prepare for it, and did not do its deeds. ﴿Then indeed Hellfire is his refuge﴾: that is, his abode, and the alif and lam are a substitute for the genitive complement. The meaning is: it is his dwelling where he settles, and his refuge to which he returns, and nothing else.

Then He mentioned the second of the two divisions, saying: ﴿But as for he who feared the position of his Lord﴾: that is, he was wary of standing before his Lord on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Rabi' said: the position of the Day of Reckoning.

Qatadah said: He says that God, mighty and majestic, has a position which the believers fear.

Mujahid said: it is his fear in this world of God, mighty and majestic, when he is about to commit a sin, so he desists from it. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And for him who fears the position of his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46]. The first is more preferable. ﴿And restrained the soul from desire﴾: that is, he held it back from inclining toward sins and forbidden things that it desires.

Muqatil said: he is the man who intends a sin, then remembers his standing for reckoning, so he abandons it.

﴿Then indeed Paradise is his refuge﴾: that is, the abode where he settles, and the place to which he returns, and nothing else.

﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its arrival?﴾: that is, when its occurrence and establishment will be.

Al-Farra' said: that is, the end of its establishment, like the anchoring of a ship.

Abu 'Ubayda said: the anchorage (mursa) of a ship is when it comes to rest. The meaning is: they ask you about the Hour, when Allah will establish it. The explanation of this has already passed in Surah al-A'raf.

﴿In what are you concerned with its mention?﴾: that is, in what matter are you, O Muhammad, concerned with mentioning the Resurrection and asking about it? The meaning is: you are not in anything of its knowledge or its mention; only God, glorified is He, knows it. This is a denial and rejection of the polytheists' question about it: that is, in what are you about this, so that they ask you about it while you do not know it.

﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾: that is, the endpoint of its knowledge, so its knowledge is not found with anyone else. This is like His saying: ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 187] and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34]. So how could they ask you about it and seek from you a clarification of the time of its establishment?

﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾: that is, a warner to whoever fears the establishment of the Hour. That is your duty; there is nothing incumbent upon you beyond it, such as informing about the time of the Hour's establishment and similar matters that Allah has kept for Himself in knowledge. He restricted the warning to those who fear, because they are the ones who benefit from warning, although he is a warner to every accountable person, Muslim and disbeliever.

The majority read "mundhiru" with the genitive construction, annexing it to what follows. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Abu Ja'far, Talhah, Ibn Muhaysin, Shaybah, al-A'raj and Humayd read it with tanwin, and this reading is narrated from Abu 'Amr.

al-Farra' said: both tanwin and its omission in "mundhir" are correct, like His saying: ﴿Accomplishing His command﴾ [al-Talaq: 3] and ﴿Weakening the plot of the disbelievers﴾ [al-Anfal: 18].

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the annexation may be to the past tense, like "darib Zayd amsi" (the one who struck Zayd yesterday).

﴿As if they, on the day they see it, had not remained but an evening or its morning﴾: that is, only the amount of the end of a day or its beginning, or the amount of the forenoon that follows that evening. The intention is to minimize the duration of the worldly life, as He said: ﴿They will feel as if they had not remained but an hour of a day﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]. It was also said that they did not remain in their graves except an evening or its morning.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the intended meaning of annexing "duha" (forenoon) to "'ashiyyah" (evening) is its annexation to the day of the evening, according to the custom of the Arabs, who say: "I will come to you in the morning or its evening, and I will come to you in the evening or its morning", so that "al-'ashiyyah" means the end of the day and "al-ghadah" means the beginning of the day.

From this is the saying of the poet:

"We attacked 'Amir in its house, with swift horses racing through both ends of its day, in the evening of the crescent moon or its last phase."

The sentence confirms what the warning implies of the swiftness of the coming of what is warned of.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿He raised its height﴾, he said: He built it. ﴿And darkened its night﴾, he said: He made its night dark.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him: ﴿And darkened its night﴾, he said: and made its night dark. ﴿And brought forth its forenoon﴾, he said: He brought forth its daylight.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾, he said: "with that."

Ibn Ḥumayd (ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd) and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also transmitted from him (Ibn ʿAbbās) that a man said to him: "There are two verses in the Book of God that contradict each other." He said: "You have only been given this because of your own opinion." The man said: "Recite ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days…﴾ until ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 9–11], and His saying ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾." He said: "God created the earth before He created the heaven, and then He spread out the earth after He had created the heaven. And His saying daḥāhā means He spread it out (basaṭahā)."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim also transmitted from him: "Daḥāhā means that He brought forth from it water and pasture, split in it the rivers, and placed in it the mountains, the sands, the paths, the hills, and what lies between them, in two days."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also transmitted from him: "al-Ṭāmma is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to ask about the Hour, so this was revealed: ﴿In what are you about its mention?﴾"

al-Bazzār, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim (who declared it ṣaḥīḥ), and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from ʿĀʾisha, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) kept asking about the Hour until God revealed ﴿In what are you about its mention?﴾ ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾, and then he stopped and no longer asked about it."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ṭabarānī, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ṭāriq ibn Shihāb, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to mention the Hour frequently until ﴿In what are you about its mention?﴾ ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾ was revealed, and then he refrained from it."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās.

al-Suyūṭī said, with a weak chain: That is, the polytheists of Mecca asked the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "When is the Hour?", mocking him. So God revealed ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its arrival?﴾, meaning its coming, ﴿In what are you about its mention?﴾, meaning: what knowledge of it do you have, O Muḥammad, ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾, meaning the final limit of its knowledge.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from ʿĀʾisha, who said: "When the Bedouins (al-aʿrāb) came to the Prophet (ﷺ), they would ask him about the Hour, and he would look at the youngest person among them and say: 'If this one lives, your Hour will come upon you.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 79, verses 27–46 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Are you the more difficult to create, or is the heaven? He constructed it.﴾ That is: is your creation after death and your resurrection more difficult in your estimation and reckoning, or the creation of the heaven? The address is to the disbelievers of Makkah, and its purpose is rebuke and silencing them, because whoever is able to create the heaven, which has this great mass and in which are the wonders of craftsmanship and the marvels of power that are evident to observers, how could He be unable to restore the bodies that He caused to die after having created them the first time? Similar to this is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ [Ghafir: 57], and His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 81]. Then He, glorified is He, explained the manner of the creation of the heaven, saying: ﴿He constructed it; He raised its height and made it proportionate.﴾ That is, He made it like a building raised above the earth. And "raised its height" means: He raised its upper part into the air.

His saying: ﴿He raised its height﴾ is an explanation of "constructed". It is said: "samaktu al-shay'" (I raised the thing), meaning I lifted it into the air, and "samuka al-shay' sumuwkan" (the thing became high), meaning it rose.

Al-Farra' said: Everything that carries something of a building or other than it is "samk", and "binaa' mamsuk" (a raised building) and "sanam samik" (a high hump), meaning high.

And al-sumuwkat (the heavens) are the heavens; from this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Indeed He who raised the sky built for us a house whose pillars are mightier and taller."

Al-Baghawi said: "raised its height" means its ceiling.

Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the sentence is complete at His saying: ﴿Or is the heaven? He constructed it﴾, because it is a relative clause of "the heaven", and the estimate is: "or the heaven which He constructed", so "alladhi" (which) is omitted, and such omission is permissible.

The meaning of ﴿and made it proportionate﴾ is: He made it even in its creation, balanced in form, with no disparity, no crookedness, no fissures and no cracks.

﴿And He darkened its night﴾: al-Ghatsh is darkness; that is, He made it dark. It is said: "ghatasha al-layl" and "aghtashahu Allah" (the night was dark, and God darkened it), just as it is said "azlama al-layl" and "azlamahu Allah". A man who is "aghtash" and a woman who is "ghatshaa" are those who cannot find their way.

Al-Raghib said: Its root is from "al-aghtash", the one who has a discharge in his eye, and from it "falat ghatsha" (a desert in which one cannot find the way); and "al-taghatush" is feigned blindness.

Al-A'sha said:

"And a dark multitude by night, in a desert without landmarks, and the sound of their driving animals comforts me."

And his saying:

"And an overwhelming one, dark-hued, covered them."

That is, the darkness of night covered them. He attributed the night to the heaven because the night occurs by the setting of the sun, and the sun is attached to the heaven.

﴿And brought forth its forenoon﴾: that is, He made its daylight shine by the illumination of the sun. He expressed the day by "al-duha" (forenoon) because it is the noblest and most pleasant of its times. He attributed it to the heaven because it becomes manifest by the appearance of the sun, which is ascribed to the heaven.

﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾: that is, after the creation of the heaven. The meaning of "dahaha" is "basaṭahā" (He spread it). This indicates that the creation of the earth came after the creation of the heaven. There is no contradiction between this verse and what preceded in Surah Fussilat, His saying: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾ [Fussilat: 11]. Rather, the reconciliation is that He, glorified is He, first created the earth not spread out, then created the heaven, then spread out the earth. We have already discussed this fully there, and we also previously discussed this at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah at His saying: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]. Some scholars of knowledge mentioned that "ba'da" (after) means "ma'a" (with), as in His saying: ﴿Violent, moreover, ignoble﴾ [al-Qalam: 13]. It was also said that "ba'da" means "qabla" (before), as in His saying: ﴿And We had certainly written in the Zabur after the Reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105], meaning before the Reminder. But the reconciliation we have mentioned is more preferable, and it is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and others, and al-Tabari chose it.

It is said: "dahautu al-shay' adhhuwhu" when I spread the thing out, and the nest of the ostrich is called "adhha" because it is spread out on the ground. Al-Mubarrad recited:

"He spread it out, and when it became level upon the water, He set the mountains upon it."

Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"And He scattered creation upon it when He spread it out, so they are its inhabitants until the calling-out."

(p-1584) Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl said:

"And I have submitted my face to Him to whom the earth submits, bearing heavy rocks."

"He spread it out, and when it became level He firmly fastened it with hands, and set the mountains upon it."

The majority read "al-ard" in the accusative under the construction of preoccupation (al-ishtighal). Al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn Maymun, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Abu Haywah, Abu al-Simak, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and Nasr ibn 'Asim read it in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (al-ibtida').

﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture﴾: that is, He caused rivers, seas and springs to gush forth from the earth, and brought forth from it its pasture, that is, the plants on which animals graze. "Mar'aha" is a mimi verbal noun, meaning its grazing, and it is originally the place of grazing. The sentence is either an explanation and elaboration of "dahaha", since settlement is not achieved by mere spreading, but rather the arrangement of the matter of subsistence, of food and drink, is necessary. Or it is in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿And the mountains He set firm﴾: that is, He established them in the earth and made them like pegs for the earth, so that it would be steady and stable and not sway with its inhabitants.

The majority read "al-jibal" in the accusative under the construction of preoccupation. Al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn Maymun, Abu Haywah, Abu al-Simak, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and Nasr ibn 'Asim read it in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence. It was said: perhaps the reason for mentioning the bringing forth of water and pasture before the setting of the mountains, although the setting is prior to it, is concern for the matter of food and drink.

﴿As a provision for you and your livestock﴾: that is, a benefit for you and your livestock, of cattle, camels and sheep. "Mata'an" is in the accusative as a verbal noun: that is, He provided you with that as a provision; or it is a verbal noun from a non-cognate verb, since His saying: ﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture﴾ carries the sense of providing with that; or it is an object of purpose: that is, He did that for the sake of providing. He said "for you and your livestock" because the benefit of what has been mentioned of the spreading, the bringing forth of water and pasture, is for them and for their livestock, and "pasture" encompasses what people and beasts eat.

﴿So when the Great Overwhelming Calamity comes﴾: that is, the great calamity that overwhelms all other calamities.

Al-Hasan and others said: it is the second blast.

Al-Dahhak and others said: it is the Resurrection, named so because it overwhelms everything due to the magnitude of its terror.

Al-Mubarrad said: "al-tammah" among the Arabs is the calamity that cannot be withstood, and it is taken, in my opinion, from their saying: "tamma al-faras tamiman" when the horse exhausts its effort in running, and "tamma al-ma'" when the water fills the whole river.

Others said: it is from "tamma al-sayl al-rakiyyah", that is, the flood buried the well; and "al-tamm" is burial.

Mujahid and others said: "al-Tammah al-Kubra" is that which sends the people of Paradise to Paradise and the people of Hellfire to Hellfire. The fa' indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes. As for the response of "idha", it was said that it is His saying: ﴿Then as for he who transgressed﴾; and it was said that it is omitted, meaning: then the matter is so, or they witness it, or they know it, or the people of the Fire are made to enter the Fire and the people of Paradise enter Paradise.

Abu al-Baqa' said: its governing element is its response, which is the meaning of ﴿the Day when man will remember what he strove﴾, for it is in the accusative by a hidden verb: that is, "I mean the day when he remembers", or "the day when he remembers, such and such will be the case." It was also said that the adverbial phrase is a substitute for "idha", and it was said it is a substitute for "al-Tammah al-Kubra". ﴿And Hellfire is brought forth for whoever sees﴾: it is conjoined to "jaat" (came). The meaning of "burrizat" is: it is made manifest, a manifestation that is hidden from no one.

Muqatil said: its covering is removed and the creatures look at it. It was also said: for whoever sees among the disbelievers, not among the believers. The apparent meaning is that it is displayed to every beholder; as for the believer, by seeing it he recognizes the extent of God's blessing upon him in being safe from it, and as for the disbeliever, his grief increases upon his grief and his regret upon his regret.

﴿As for him who transgressed﴾: that is, exceeded the limit in disbelief and sins.

﴿And preferred the worldly life﴾: that is, he put it ahead of the Hereafter, did not prepare for it, and did not do its deeds. ﴿Then indeed Hellfire is his refuge﴾: that is, his abode, and the alif and lam are a substitute for the genitive complement. Al-Rabi' said: the position of the Day of Reckoning.

Mujahid said: it is his fear in this world of God, mighty and majestic, when he is about to commit a sin, so he desists from it. Muqatil said: he is the man who intends a sin, then remembers his standing for reckoning, so he abandons it.

﴿Then indeed Paradise is his refuge﴾: that is, the abode where he settles, and the place to which he returns, and nothing else.

﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its arrival?﴾: that is, when its occurrence and establishment will be.

Al-Farra' said: that is, the end of its establishment, like the anchoring of a ship.

Abu 'Ubayda said: the anchorage (mursa) of a ship is when it comes to rest. The meaning is: they ask you about the Hour, when Allah will establish it. The explanation of this has already passed in Surah al-A'raf.

﴿In what are you concerned with its mention?﴾: that is, in what matter are you, O Muhammad, concerned with mentioning the Resurrection and asking about it? So God revealed ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its arrival?﴾, meaning its coming, ﴿In what are you about its mention?﴾, meaning: what knowledge of it do you have, O Muḥammad, ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾, meaning the final limit of its knowledge.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from ʿĀʾisha, who said: "When the Bedouins (al-aʿrāb) came to the Prophet (ﷺ), they would ask him about the Hour, and he would look at the youngest person among them and say: 'If this one lives, your Hour will come upon you.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 79, verses 27–46 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Are you the more difficult to create, or is the heaven? He constructed it.﴾ That is: is your creation after death and your resurrection more difficult in your estimation and reckoning, or the creation of the heaven? The address is to the disbelievers of Makkah, and its purpose is rebuke and silencing them, because whoever is able to create the heaven, which has this great mass and in which are the wonders of craftsmanship and the marvels of power that are evident to observers, how could He be unable to restore the bodies that He caused to die after having created them the first time? Similar to this is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ [Ghafir: 57], and His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 81]. Then He, glorified is He, explained the manner of the creation of the heaven, saying: ﴿He constructed it; He raised its height and made it proportionate.﴾ That is, He made it like a building raised above the earth. And "raised its height" means: He raised its upper part into the air.

His saying: ﴿He raised its height﴾ is an explanation of "constructed". It is said: "samaktu al-shay'" (I raised the thing), meaning I lifted it into the air, and "samuka al-shay' sumuwkan" (the thing became high), meaning it rose.

Al-Farra' said: Everything that carries something of a building or other than it is "samk", and "binaa' mamsuk" (a raised building) and "sanam samik" (a high hump), meaning high.

And al-sumuwkat (the heavens) are the heavens; from this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Indeed He who raised the sky built for us a house whose pillars are mightier and taller."

Al-Baghawi said: "raised its height" means its ceiling.

Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the sentence is complete at His saying: ﴿Or is the heaven? He constructed it﴾, because it is a relative clause of "the heaven", and the estimate is: "or the heaven which He constructed", so "alladhi" (which) is omitted, and such omission is permissible.

The meaning of ﴿and made it proportionate﴾ is: He made it even in its creation, balanced in form, with no disparity, no crookedness, no fissures and no cracks.

﴿And He darkened its night﴾: al-Ghatsh is darkness; that is, He made it dark. It is said: "ghatasha al-layl" and "aghtashahu Allah" (the night was dark, and God darkened it), just as it is said "azlama al-layl" and "azlamahu Allah". A man who is "aghtash" and a woman who is "ghatshaa" are those who cannot find their way.

Al-Raghib said: Its root is from "al-aghtash", the one who has a discharge in his eye, and from it "falat ghatsha" (a desert in which one cannot find the way); and "al-taghatush" is feigned blindness.

Al-A'sha said:

"And a dark multitude by night, in a desert without landmarks, and the sound of their driving animals comforts me."

And his saying:

"And an overwhelming one, dark-hued, covered them."

That is, the darkness of night covered them. He attributed the night to the heaven because the night occurs by the setting of the sun, and the sun is attached to the heaven.

﴿And brought forth its forenoon﴾: that is, He made its daylight shine by the illumination of the sun. He expressed the day by "al-duha" (forenoon) because it is the noblest and most pleasant of its times. He attributed it to the heaven because it becomes manifest by the appearance of the sun, which is ascribed to the heaven.

﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾: that is, after the creation of the heaven. The meaning of "dahaha" is "basaṭahā" (He spread it). This indicates that the creation of the earth came after the creation of the heaven. There is no contradiction between this verse and what preceded in Surah Fussilat, His saying: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾ [Fussilat: 11]. Rather, the reconciliation is that He, glorified is He, first created the earth not spread out, then created the heaven, then spread out the earth. We have already discussed this fully there, and we also previously discussed this at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah at His saying: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]. Some scholars of knowledge mentioned that "ba'da" (after) means "ma'a" (with), as in His saying: ﴿Violent, moreover, ignoble﴾ [al-Qalam: 13]. It was also said that "ba'da" means "qabla" (before), as in His saying: ﴿And We had certainly written in the Zabur after the Reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105], meaning before the Reminder. But the reconciliation we have mentioned is more preferable, and it is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and others, and al-Tabari chose it.

It is said: "dahautu al-shay' adhhuwhu" when I spread the thing out, and the nest of the ostrich is called "adhha" because it is spread out on the ground. Al-Mubarrad recited:

"He spread it out, and when it became level upon the water, He set the mountains upon it."

Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"And He scattered creation upon it when He spread it out, so they are its inhabitants until the calling-out."

(p-1584) Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl said:

"And I have submitted my face to Him to whom the earth submits, bearing heavy rocks."

"He spread it out, and when it became level He firmly fastened it with hands, and set the mountains upon it."

The majority read "al-ard" in the accusative under the construction of preoccupation (al-ishtighal). Al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn Maymun, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Abu Haywah, Abu al-Simak, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and Nasr ibn 'Asim read it in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (al-ibtida').

﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture﴾: that is, He caused rivers, seas and springs to gush forth from the earth, and brought forth from it its pasture, that is, the plants on which animals graze. "Mar'aha" is a mimi verbal noun, meaning its grazing, and it is originally the place of grazing. The sentence is either an explanation and elaboration of "dahaha", since settlement is not achieved by mere spreading, but rather the arrangement of the matter of subsistence, of food and drink, is necessary. Or it is in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿And the mountains He set firm﴾: that is, He established them in the earth and made them like pegs for the earth, so that it would be steady and stable and not sway with its inhabitants.

The majority read "al-jibal" in the accusative under the construction of preoccupation. Al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn Maymun, Abu Haywah, Abu al-Simak, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and Nasr ibn 'Asim read it in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence. It was said: perhaps the reason for mentioning the bringing forth of water and pasture before the setting of the mountains, although the setting is prior to it, is concern for the matter of food and drink.

﴿As a provision for you and your livestock﴾: that is, a benefit for you and your livestock, of cattle, camels and sheep. "Mata'an" is in the accusative as a verbal noun: that is, He provided you with that as a provision; or it is a verbal noun from a non-cognate verb, since His saying: ﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture﴾ carries the sense of providing with that; or it is an object of purpose: that is, He did that for the sake of providing. He said "for you and your livestock" because the benefit of what has been mentioned of the spreading, the bringing forth of water and pasture, is for them and for their livestock, and "pasture" encompasses what people and beasts eat.

﴿So when the Great Overwhelming Calamity comes﴾: that is, the great calamity that overwhelms all other calamities.

Al-Hasan and others said: it is the second blast.

Al-Dahhak and others said: it is the Resurrection, named so because it overwhelms everything due to the magnitude of its terror.

Al-Mubarrad said: "al-tammah" among the Arabs is the calamity that cannot be withstood, and it is taken, in my opinion, from their saying: "tamma al-faras tamiman" when the horse exhausts its effort in running, and "tamma al-ma'" when the water fills the whole river.

Others said: it is from "tamma al-sayl al-rakiyyah", that is, the flood buried the well; and "al-tamm" is burial.

Mujahid and others said: "al-Tammah al-Kubra" is that which sends the people of Paradise to Paradise and the people of Hellfire to Hellfire. The fa' indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes. As for the response of "idha", it was said that it is His saying: ﴿Then as for he who transgressed﴾; and it was said that it is omitted, meaning: then the matter is so, or they witness it, or they know it, or the people of the Fire are made to enter the Fire and the people of Paradise enter Paradise.

Abu al-Baqa' said: its governing element is its response, which is the meaning of ﴿the Day when man will remember what he strove﴾, for it is in the accusative by a hidden verb: that is, "I mean the day when he remembers", or "the day when he remembers, such and such will be the case." It was also said that the adverbial phrase is a substitute for "idha", and it was said it is a substitute for "al-Tammah al-Kubra". The meaning of "man remembers what he strove" is that he remembers what he did of good or evil, because he sees it recorded in the pages of his deeds; and "ma" is either a verbal source or a relative pronoun.

﴿And Hellfire is brought forth for whoever sees﴾: it is conjoined to "jaat" (came). The meaning of "burrizat" is: it is made manifest, a manifestation that is hidden from no one.

Muqatil said: its covering is removed and the creatures look at it. It was also said: for whoever sees among the disbelievers, not among the believers. The apparent meaning is that it is displayed to every beholder; as for the believer, by seeing it he recognizes the extent of God's blessing upon him in being safe from it, and as for the disbeliever, his grief increases upon his grief and his regret upon his regret.

The majority read "li-man yara" with the verb in the third person masculine (yā'), while 'A'isha, Malik ibn Dinar, 'Ikrimah and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with the second person (tā'): that is, Hellfire is made to see whoever it sees, or it is made to see you, O Muhammad.

Ibn Mas'ud read "li-man ra'a" in the past tense form of the verb.

﴿As for him who transgressed﴾: that is, exceeded the limit in disbelief and sins.

﴿And preferred the worldly life﴾: that is, he put it ahead of the Hereafter, did not prepare for it, and did not do its deeds. ﴿Then indeed Hellfire is his refuge﴾: that is, his abode, and the alif and lam are a substitute for the genitive complement. The meaning is: it is his dwelling where he settles, and his refuge to which he returns, and nothing else.

Then He mentioned the second of the two divisions, saying: ﴿But as for he who feared the position of his Lord﴾: that is, he was wary of standing before his Lord on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Rabi' said: the position of the Day of Reckoning.

Qatadah said: He says that God, mighty and majestic, has a position which the believers fear.

Mujahid said: it is his fear in this world of God, mighty and majestic, when he is about to commit a sin, so he desists from it. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And for him who fears the position of his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46]. The first is more preferable. ﴿And restrained the soul from desire﴾: that is, he held it back from inclining toward sins and forbidden things that it desires.

Muqatil said: he is the man who intends a sin, then remembers his standing for reckoning, so he abandons it.

﴿Then indeed Paradise is his refuge﴾: that is, the abode where he settles, and the place to which he returns, and nothing else.

﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its arrival?﴾: that is, when its occurrence and establishment will be.

Al-Farra' said: that is, the end of its establishment, like the anchoring of a ship.

Abu 'Ubayda said: the anchorage (mursa) of a ship is when it comes to rest. The meaning is: they ask you about the Hour, when Allah will establish it. The explanation of this has already passed in Surah al-A'raf.

﴿In what are you concerned with its mention?﴾: that is, in what matter are you, O Muhammad, concerned with mentioning the Resurrection and asking about it? The meaning is: you are not in anything of its knowledge or its mention; only God, glorified is He, knows it. This is a denial and rejection of the polytheists' question about it: that is, in what are you about this, so that they ask you about it while you do not know it.

﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾: that is, the endpoint of its knowledge, so its knowledge is not found with anyone else. This is like His saying: ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 187] and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34]. So how could they ask you about it and seek from you a clarification of the time of its establishment?

﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾: that is, a warner to whoever fears the establishment of the Hour. That is your duty; there is nothing incumbent upon you beyond it, such as informing about the time of the Hour's establishment and similar matters that Allah has kept for Himself in knowledge. He restricted the warning to those who fear, because they are the ones who benefit from warning, although he is a warner to every accountable person, Muslim and disbeliever.

The majority read "mundhiru" with the genitive construction, annexing it to what follows. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Abu Ja'far, Talhah, Ibn Muhaysin, Shaybah, al-A'raj and Humayd read it with tanwin, and this reading is narrated from Abu 'Amr.

al-Farra' said: both tanwin and its omission in "mundhir" are correct, like His saying: ﴿Accomplishing His command﴾ [al-Talaq: 3] and ﴿Weakening the plot of the disbelievers﴾ [al-Anfal: 18].

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the annexation may be to the past tense, like "darib Zayd amsi" (the one who struck Zayd yesterday).

﴿As if they, on the day they see it, had not remained but an evening or its morning﴾: that is, only the amount of the end of a day or its beginning, or the amount of the forenoon that follows that evening. The intention is to minimize the duration of the worldly life, as He said: ﴿They will feel as if they had not remained but an hour of a day﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]. It was also said that they did not remain in their graves except an evening or its morning.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the intended meaning of annexing "duha" (forenoon) to "'ashiyyah" (evening) is its annexation to the day of the evening, according to the custom of the Arabs, who say: "I will come to you in the morning or its evening, and I will come to you in the evening or its morning", so that "al-'ashiyyah" means the end of the day and "al-ghadah" means the beginning of the day.

From this is the saying of the poet:

"We attacked 'Amir in its house, with swift horses racing through both ends of its day, in the evening of the crescent moon or its last phase."

The sentence confirms what the warning implies of the swiftness of the coming of what is warned of.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿He raised its height﴾, he said: He built it. ﴿And darkened its night﴾, he said: He made its night dark.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him: ﴿And darkened its night﴾, he said: and made its night dark. ﴿And brought forth its forenoon﴾, he said: He brought forth its daylight.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾, he said: "with that."

Ibn Ḥumayd (ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd) and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also transmitted from him (Ibn ʿAbbās) that a man said to him: "There are two verses in the Book of God that contradict each other." He said: "You have only been given this because of your own opinion." The man said: "Recite ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days…﴾ until ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 9–11], and His saying ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾." He said: "God created the earth before He created the heaven, and then He spread out the earth after He had created the heaven. And His saying daḥāhā means He spread it out (basaṭahā)."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim also transmitted from him: "Daḥāhā means that He brought forth from it water and pasture, split in it the rivers, and placed in it the mountains, the sands, the paths, the hills, and what lies between them, in two days."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also transmitted from him: "al-Ṭāmma is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to ask about the Hour, so this was revealed: ﴿In what are you about its mention?﴾"

al-Bazzār, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim (who declared it ṣaḥīḥ), and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from ʿĀʾisha, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) kept asking about the Hour until God revealed ﴿In what are you about its mention?﴾ ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾, and then he stopped and no longer asked about it."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ṭabarānī, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ṭāriq ibn Shihāb, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to mention the Hour frequently until ﴿In what are you about its mention?﴾ ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾ was revealed, and then he refrained from it."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās.

al-Suyūṭī said, with a weak chain: That is, the polytheists of Mecca asked the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "When is the Hour?", mocking him. So God revealed ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its arrival?﴾, meaning its coming, ﴿In what are you about its mention?﴾, meaning: what knowledge of it do you have, O Muḥammad, ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾, meaning the final limit of its knowledge.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from ʿĀʾisha, who said: "When the Bedouins (al-aʿrāb) came to the Prophet (ﷺ), they would ask him about the Hour, and he would look at the youngest person among them and say: 'If this one lives, your Hour will come upon you.'"

Abu al-Baqa' said: its governing element is its response, which is the meaning of ﴿the Day when man will remember what he strove﴾, for it is in the accusative by a hidden verb: that is, "I mean the day when he remembers", or "the day when he remembers, such and such will be the case." It was also said that the adverbial phrase is a substitute for "idha", and it was said it is a substitute for "al-Tammah al-Kubra". The meaning of "man remembers what he strove" is that he remembers what he did of good or evil, because he sees it recorded in the pages of his deeds; and "ma" is either a verbal source or a relative pronoun.

﴿And Hellfire is brought forth for whoever sees﴾: it is conjoined to "jaat" (came). The meaning of "burrizat" is: it is made manifest, a manifestation that is hidden from no one.

Muqatil said: its covering is removed and the creatures look at it. It was also said: for whoever sees among the disbelievers, not among the believers. The apparent meaning is that it is displayed to every beholder; as for the believer, by seeing it he recognizes the extent of God's blessing upon him in being safe from it, and as for the disbeliever, his grief increases upon his grief and his regret upon his regret.

The majority read "li-man yara" with the verb in the third person masculine (yā'), while 'A'isha, Malik ibn Dinar, 'Ikrimah and Zayd ibn 'Ali read it with the second person (tā'): that is, Hellfire is made to see whoever it sees, or it is made to see you, O Muhammad.

Ibn Mas'ud read "li-man ra'a" in the past tense form of the verb.

﴿As for him who transgressed﴾: that is, exceeded the limit in disbelief and sins.

﴿And preferred the worldly life﴾: that is, he put it ahead of the Hereafter, did not prepare for it, and did not do its deeds. ﴿Then indeed Hellfire is his refuge﴾: that is, his abode, and the alif and lam are a substitute for the genitive complement. The meaning is: it is his dwelling where he settles, and his refuge to which he returns, and nothing else.

Then He mentioned the second of the two divisions, saying: ﴿But as for he who feared the position of his Lord﴾: that is, he was wary of standing before his Lord on the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Rabi' said: the position of the Day of Reckoning.

Qatadah said: He says that God, mighty and majestic, has a position which the believers fear.

Mujahid said: it is his fear in this world of God, mighty and majestic, when he is about to commit a sin, so he desists from it. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And for him who fears the position of his Lord are two gardens﴾ [al-Rahman: 46]. The first is more preferable. ﴿And restrained the soul from desire﴾: that is, he held it back from inclining toward sins and forbidden things that it desires.

Muqatil said: he is the man who intends a sin, then remembers his standing for reckoning, so he abandons it.

﴿Then indeed Paradise is his refuge﴾: that is, the abode where he settles, and the place to which he returns, and nothing else.

﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its arrival?﴾: that is, when its occurrence and establishment will be.

Al-Farra' said: that is, the end of its establishment, like the anchoring of a ship.

Abu 'Ubayda said: the anchorage (mursa) of a ship is when it comes to rest. The meaning is: they ask you about the Hour, when Allah will establish it. The explanation of this has already passed in Surah al-A'raf.

﴿In what are you concerned with its mention?﴾: that is, in what matter are you, O Muhammad, concerned with mentioning the Resurrection and asking about it? The meaning is: you are not in anything of its knowledge or its mention; only God, glorified is He, knows it. This is a denial and rejection of the polytheists' question about it: that is, in what are you about this, so that they ask you about it while you do not know it.

﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾: that is, the endpoint of its knowledge, so its knowledge is not found with anyone else. This is like His saying: ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 187] and His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour﴾ [Luqman: 34]. So how could they ask you about it and seek from you a clarification of the time of its establishment?

﴿You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾: that is, a warner to whoever fears the establishment of the Hour. That is your duty; there is nothing incumbent upon you beyond it, such as informing about the time of the Hour's establishment and similar matters that Allah has kept for Himself in knowledge. He restricted the warning to those who fear, because they are the ones who benefit from warning, although he is a warner to every accountable person, Muslim and disbeliever.

The majority read "mundhiru" with the genitive construction, annexing it to what follows. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, Abu Ja'far, Talhah, Ibn Muhaysin, Shaybah, al-A'raj and Humayd read it with tanwin, and this reading is narrated from Abu 'Amr.

al-Farra' said: both tanwin and its omission in "mundhir" are correct, like His saying: ﴿Accomplishing His command﴾ [al-Talaq: 3] and ﴿Weakening the plot of the disbelievers﴾ [al-Anfal: 18].

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the annexation may be to the past tense, like "darib Zayd amsi" (the one who struck Zayd yesterday).

﴿As if they, on the day they see it, had not remained but an evening or its morning﴾: that is, only the amount of the end of a day or its beginning, or the amount of the forenoon that follows that evening. The intention is to minimize the duration of the worldly life, as He said: ﴿They will feel as if they had not remained but an hour of a day﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 35]. It was also said that they did not remain in their graves except an evening or its morning.

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the intended meaning of annexing "duha" (forenoon) to "'ashiyyah" (evening) is its annexation to the day of the evening, according to the custom of the Arabs, who say: "I will come to you in the morning or its evening, and I will come to you in the evening or its morning", so that "al-'ashiyyah" means the end of the day and "al-ghadah" means the beginning of the day.

From this is the saying of the poet:

"We attacked 'Amir in its house, with swift horses racing through both ends of its day, in the evening of the crescent moon or its last phase."

The sentence confirms what the warning implies of the swiftness of the coming of what is warned of.

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿He raised its height﴾, he said: He built it. ﴿And darkened its night﴾, he said: He made its night dark.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him: ﴿And darkened its night﴾, he said: and made its night dark. ﴿And brought forth its forenoon﴾, he said: He brought forth its daylight.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: ﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾, he said: "with that."

Ibn Ḥumayd (ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd) and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also transmitted from him (Ibn ʿAbbās) that a man said to him: "There are two verses in the Book of God that contradict each other." He said: "You have only been given this because of your own opinion." The man said: "Recite ﴿Say: Do you indeed disbelieve in the One who created the earth in two days…﴾ until ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 9–11], and His saying ﴿And after that He spread out the earth﴾." He said: "God created the earth before He created the heaven, and then He spread out the earth after He had created the heaven. And His saying daḥāhā means He spread it out (basaṭahā)."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim also transmitted from him: "Daḥāhā means that He brought forth from it water and pasture, split in it the rivers, and placed in it the mountains, the sands, the paths, the hills, and what lies between them, in two days."

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also transmitted from him: "al-Ṭāmma is one of the names of the Day of Resurrection."

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to ask about the Hour, so this was revealed: ﴿In what are you about its mention?﴾"

al-Bazzār, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḥākim (who declared it ṣaḥīḥ), and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from ʿĀʾisha, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) kept asking about the Hour until God revealed ﴿In what are you about its mention?﴾ ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾, and then he stopped and no longer asked about it."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Nasāʾī, Ibn Jarīr, al-Ṭabarānī, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ṭāriq ibn Shihāb, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to mention the Hour frequently until ﴿In what are you about its mention?﴾ ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾ was revealed, and then he refrained from it."

Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās.

al-Suyūṭī said, with a weak chain: That is, the polytheists of Mecca asked the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "When is the Hour?", mocking him. So God revealed ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its arrival?﴾, meaning its coming, ﴿In what are you about its mention?﴾, meaning: what knowledge of it do you have, O Muḥammad, ﴿To your Lord is its finality﴾, meaning the final limit of its knowledge.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from ʿĀʾisha, who said: "When the Bedouins (al-aʿrāb) came to the Prophet (ﷺ), they would ask him about the Hour, and he would look at the youngest person among them and say: 'If this one lives, your Hour will come upon you.'"

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 79, verses 27–46 (part 1 of 2):

His saying: ﴿Are you the more difficult to create, or is the heaven? He constructed it.﴾ That is: is your creation after death and your resurrection more difficult in your estimation and reckoning, or the creation of the heaven? The address is to the disbelievers of Makkah, and its purpose is rebuke and silencing them, because whoever is able to create the heaven, which has this great mass and in which are the wonders of craftsmanship and the marvels of power that are evident to observers, how could He be unable to restore the bodies that He caused to die after having created them the first time? Similar to this is His saying, glorified is He: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾ [Ghafir: 57], and His saying: ﴿Is not He who created the heavens and the earth able to create the likes of them?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 81]. Then He, glorified is He, explained the manner of the creation of the heaven, saying: ﴿He constructed it; He raised its height and made it proportionate.﴾ That is, He made it like a building raised above the earth. And "raised its height" means: He raised its upper part into the air.

His saying: ﴿He raised its height﴾ is an explanation of "constructed". It is said: "samaktu al-shay'" (I raised the thing), meaning I lifted it into the air, and "samuka al-shay' sumuwkan" (the thing became high), meaning it rose.

Al-Farra' said: Everything that carries something of a building or other than it is "samk", and "binaa' mamsuk" (a raised building) and "sanam samik" (a high hump), meaning high.

And al-sumuwkat (the heavens) are the heavens; from this is the saying of al-Farazdaq:

"Indeed He who raised the sky built for us a house whose pillars are mightier and taller."

Al-Baghawi said: "raised its height" means its ceiling.

Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the sentence is complete at His saying: ﴿Or is the heaven? He constructed it﴾, because it is a relative clause of "the heaven", and the estimate is: "or the heaven which He constructed", so "alladhi" (which) is omitted, and such omission is permissible.

The meaning of ﴿and made it proportionate﴾ is: He made it even in its creation, balanced in form, with no disparity, no crookedness, no fissures and no cracks.

﴿And He darkened its night﴾: al-Ghatsh is darkness; that is, He made it dark. It is said: "ghatasha al-layl" and "aghtashahu Allah" (the night was dark, and God darkened it), just as it is said "azlama al-layl" and "azlamahu Allah". A man who is "aghtash" and a woman who is "ghatshaa" are those who cannot find their way.

Al-Raghib said: Its root is from "al-aghtash", the one who has a discharge in his eye, and from it "falat ghatsha" (a desert in which one cannot find the way); and "al-taghatush" is feigned blindness.

Al-A'sha said:

"And a dark multitude by night, in a desert without landmarks, and the sound of their driving animals comforts me."

And his saying:

"And an overwhelming one, dark-hued, covered them."

That is, the darkness of night covered them. He attributed the night to the heaven because the night occurs by the setting of the sun, and the sun is attached to the heaven.

﴿And brought forth its forenoon﴾: that is, He made its daylight shine by the illumination of the sun. He expressed the day by "al-duha" (forenoon) because it is the noblest and most pleasant of its times. He attributed it to the heaven because it becomes manifest by the appearance of the sun, which is ascribed to the heaven.

﴿And the earth after that He spread out﴾: that is, after the creation of the heaven. The meaning of "dahaha" is "basaṭahā" (He spread it). This indicates that the creation of the earth came after the creation of the heaven. There is no contradiction between this verse and what preceded in Surah Fussilat, His saying: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾ [Fussilat: 11]. Rather, the reconciliation is that He, glorified is He, first created the earth not spread out, then created the heaven, then spread out the earth. We have already discussed this fully there, and we also previously discussed this at the beginning of Surah al-Baqarah at His saying: ﴿It is He who created for you all that is on the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 29]. Some scholars of knowledge mentioned that "ba'da" (after) means "ma'a" (with), as in His saying: ﴿Violent, moreover, ignoble﴾ [al-Qalam: 13]. It was also said that "ba'da" means "qabla" (before), as in His saying: ﴿And We had certainly written in the Zabur after the Reminder﴾ [al-Anbiya': 105], meaning before the Reminder. But the reconciliation we have mentioned is more preferable, and it is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and others, and al-Tabari chose it.

It is said: "dahautu al-shay' adhhuwhu" when I spread the thing out, and the nest of the ostrich is called "adhha" because it is spread out on the ground. Al-Mubarrad recited:

"He spread it out, and when it became level upon the water, He set the mountains upon it."

Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"And He scattered creation upon it when He spread it out, so they are its inhabitants until the calling-out."

(p-1584) Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl said:

"And I have submitted my face to Him to whom the earth submits, bearing heavy rocks."

"He spread it out, and when it became level He firmly fastened it with hands, and set the mountains upon it."

The majority read "al-ard" in the accusative under the construction of preoccupation (al-ishtighal). Al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn Maymun, Ibn Abi 'Abla, Abu Haywah, Abu al-Simak, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and Nasr ibn 'Asim read it in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (al-ibtida').

﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture﴾: that is, He caused rivers, seas and springs to gush forth from the earth, and brought forth from it its pasture, that is, the plants on which animals graze. "Mar'aha" is a mimi verbal noun, meaning its grazing, and it is originally the place of grazing. The sentence is either an explanation and elaboration of "dahaha", since settlement is not achieved by mere spreading, but rather the arrangement of the matter of subsistence, of food and drink, is necessary. Or it is in the place of the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal).

﴿And the mountains He set firm﴾: that is, He established them in the earth and made them like pegs for the earth, so that it would be steady and stable and not sway with its inhabitants.

The majority read "al-jibal" in the accusative under the construction of preoccupation. Al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn Maymun, Abu Haywah, Abu al-Simak, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and Nasr ibn 'Asim read it in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence. It was said: perhaps the reason for mentioning the bringing forth of water and pasture before the setting of the mountains, although the setting is prior to it, is concern for the matter of food and drink.

﴿As a provision for you and your livestock﴾: that is, a benefit for you and your livestock, of cattle, camels and sheep. "Mata'an" is in the accusative as a verbal noun: that is, He provided you with that as a provision; or it is a verbal noun from a non-cognate verb, since His saying: ﴿He brought forth from it its water and its pasture﴾ carries the sense of providing with that; or it is an object of purpose: that is, He did that for the sake of providing. He said "for you and your livestock" because the benefit of what has been mentioned of the spreading, the bringing forth of water and pasture, is for them and for their livestock, and "pasture" encompasses what people and beasts eat.

﴿So when the Great Overwhelming Calamity comes﴾: that is, the great calamity that overwhelms all other calamities.

Al-Hasan and others said: it is the second blast.

Al-Dahhak and others said: it is the Resurrection, named so because it overwhelms everything due to the magnitude of its terror.

Al-Mubarrad said: "al-tammah" among the Arabs is the calamity that cannot be withstood, and it is taken, in my opinion, from their saying: "tamma al-faras tamiman" when the horse exhausts its effort in running, and "tamma al-ma'" when the water fills the whole river.

Others said: it is from "tamma al-sayl al-rakiyyah", that is, the flood buried the well; and "al-tamm" is burial.

Mujahid and others said: "al-Tammah al-Kubra" is that which sends the people of Paradise to Paradise and the people of Hellfire to Hellfire. The fa' indicates the sequence of what follows upon what precedes. As for the response of "idha", it was said that it is His saying: ﴿Then as for he who transgressed﴾; and it was said that it is omitted, meaning: then the matter is so, or they witness it, or they know it, or the people of the Fire are made to enter the Fire and the people of Paradise enter Paradise.

Muqatil said: its covering is removed and the creatures look at it. It was also said: for whoever sees among the disbelievers, not among the believers. The apparent meaning is that it is displayed to every beholder; as for the believer, by seeing it he recognizes the extent of God's blessing upon him in being safe from it, and as for the disbeliever, his grief increases upon his grief and his regret upon his regret.

﴿As for him who transgressed﴾: that is, exceeded the limit in disbelief and sins.

Al-Rabi' said: the position of the Day of Reckoning.

﴿Then indeed Paradise is his refuge﴾: that is, the abode where he settles, and the place to which he returns, and nothing else.

﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its arrival?﴾: that is, when its occurrence and establishment will be.

Al-Farra' said: that is, the end of its establishment, like the anchoring of a ship.

Abu 'Ubayda said: the anchorage (mursa) of a ship is when it comes to rest. The meaning is: they ask you about the Hour, when Allah will establish it. The explanation of this has already passed in Surah al-A'raf.
